title: Basis for preparation
heading: 1.1 Basis for preparation
start_phrase: Our Sustainability Statement for the year ended 31 December 2024 comprises ING Groep N.V. (the p arent company ) and its subsidiaries, together referred to as ING Group, in line with the consolidation of our Financial Statements as included in Note 1 ‘Basis of preparation and material accounting policy information’.
summary:
- First Sustainability Statement prepared in accordance with ESRS, applied voluntarily as CSRD is not yet transposed into Dutch law.
- Acknowledges market adaptation challenges: limited data availability/reliability, absence of industry-specific guidance, and uncertainties around relevance and comparability.
- Basis for preparation: covers ING Groep N.V. and subsidiaries, aligned with consolidated financial statements; prepared per ESRS and the outcome of a double materiality assessment (DMA).
- DMA performed following ESRS and EFRAG guidance, covering own operations and the full value chain; identifies material topics and related impacts, risks, and opportunities across Environment, Social, and Governance; includes an EU Taxonomy summary and mandatory tables in the Appendix to the Executive Board report.
- Uncertainties and estimations: first-year implementation, evolving guidance, lack of comparatives, need to embed processes and strengthen internal controls; data limitations expected to improve over time with iterative refinements.
- Reliance on estimates and external data vendors for emissions and other ESG metrics; vendor controls are generally unaudited; ING conducts its own data quality reviews but residual risks remain; metrics may be updated as better data becomes available; appendix provides metric-level details.
- Connectivity with financial statements: monetary amounts for financed emissions, intensity metrics, and transition/physical risk disclosures are derived from the credit risk portfolio (sometimes including uncommitted limits), subject to internal data standards; transition risk provisioning updated with a management adjustment to reflect expected credit losses in the current business lending portfolio.
- Placement and structure: excerpt sits within the ING Group Annual Report 2024 and references the broader report contents (strategy, governance, sustainability statement, risk and capital management, and financial statements).
text:
Our Sustainability Statement for the year ended 31 December 2024 comprises ING Groep N.V. (the p arent  
company ) and its subsidiaries, together referred to as ING Group, in line with the consolidation of our 
Financial Statements  as included in Note 1 ‘Basis of preparation and material accounting policy information’.  
We have prepared the Sustainability Statement in accordance with the European Sustainability Reporting 
Standard  (ESRS)  and based on the outcome of our double materiality a ssessment  (DMA) .
Our DMA has been performed in accordance with ESRS, supported by the EFRAG implementation guidance, 
covering our own operations and our upstream and downstream value chain, which is explained further in 
our ‘ Business model and strategy ’ section. The DMA concludes on our material topic s and the related  
impacts, risks and opportunities (IRO s), which we have disclosed in the respective ‘ Environment ’, ‘Social ’ and 
‘Governance ’ sections. As required by ESRS, and in line with our previous year reporting, we have included a 
summary on the EU Taxonomy within our ' Environment ' section and included the mandatory tables in the 
‘Appendix to the Executive Board report ’.

title: Uncertainties and estimations
heading: 1.2 Uncertainties and estimations
start_phrase: The implementation of the CSRD comes with several uncertainties as we navigate this new regulatory landscape.
summary:
- First ESRS-aligned Sustainability Statement for ING Group (year ended 31 December 2024), applied voluntarily as CSRD is not yet transposed into Dutch law.
- Acknowledges market-wide challenges: limited data availability and reliability, lack of industry-specific guidance, and uncertainties affecting relevance and comparability.
- Basis for preparation: covers ING Groep N.V. and subsidiaries (aligned with financial statement consolidation); prepared in accordance with ESRS and informed by a double materiality assessment (DMA) following EFRAG guidance, spanning own operations and the full value chain.
- DMA outcomes: identification of material topics and related impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs), disclosed across Environment, Social, and Governance sections; inclusion of an EU Taxonomy summary and mandatory tables in the Appendix to the Executive Board report.
- Uncertainties and estimations: first-year application, evolving guidance, no comparative figures, ongoing integration into processes and internal controls, and data limitations. Reliance on external data vendors for emissions and ESG metrics; vendor methodologies generally unaudited. ING performs internal data quality reviews but notes residual risks of inaccuracies; expects to refine reporting as standards and data quality improve. Metric-level details in the Appendix.
- Connectivity to financial statements: monetary figures for financed emissions, emissions intensity, and transition/physical risks are derived from the credit risk portfolio (sometimes including uncommitted limits) and adhere to internal data standards. Transition risk provisions updated via a management adjustment to reflect expected credit losses in the current business lending portfolio.
- Includes pointers to broader report structure (e.g., strategy, governance, risk management, financial statements, and appendices).
text:
The implementation of the CSRD comes with several uncertainties as we navigate this new regulatory 
landscape. As this is the first reporting, there is a lack of prior experience in applying the new requirements. 
Additionally, guidance is still evolving, and an industry-specific standard is lacking, making interpretation and 
implementation more complex. The absence of comparative figures under the new requirements further 
complicates benchmarking and trend analysis. Moreover, sustainability reporting needs to be fully 
embedded into ING’s existing processes and procedures, requiring adjustments and further enhancement of 
our internal control environment. Data limitations remain a key challenge, as we work towards improving 
the accuracy, completeness, and consistency of sustainability information. As a result, ING is expected to 
refine the reporting approach over time as best practices, regulatory expectations, and market standards 
develop.
The evolving stage of the market for sustainability reporting necessitates the reliance on estimates, due to 
the ongoing development of standardised metrics and comprehensive data collection practices. We mainly 
utilise external data vendors for the sourcing of emissions data and estimates, as well as other ESG-related 
information, risk information and emission -intensity metrics.
Our data vendors perform data reliability procedures and controls before submitting the data to ING. These 
processes and the underlying models and methodologies are generally not audited, which means that 
despite their internal control procedures, data limitation s may still exist. At ING, we perform our own data 
quality reviews and controls on the received data, including the assessment of historical trends and 
engaging with the vendors on potential outliers and observations. There is always a risk of applying 
inaccurate and/or incomplete data. We continue our efforts to limit this as much as possible and as long as 
the market evolves, and data quality matures, we may refine and update our measurements based on new, 
more accurate and/or more granular data becoming available in the future. See  the ‘Appendix to the 
Executive Board report ’ for more details per metric.

text:
Business model and strategy
Our strategy is about growing the difference by providing superior value for our customers and putting 
sustainability at the heart of what we do. With our business we provide services to our Retail  and Wholesale 
clients, worldwide.  For more information on our  operating environment and strategy, see sections ‘ ING at a 
glance ’ and  ‘Strategy, business model and value creation ’. This section provides an overview of our identified 
material impacts, risks and opportunities, how these interact with our strategy and business model, and 
insights into the methodology of our DMA.

title: Our value chain
heading: 2.1 Our value chain
start_phrase: With a view to comprehensively captur e impacts, risks and opportunities, the DMA has to focus on the most significant activities, services and products.
summary:
- Strategic focus: grow by delivering superior customer value with sustainability embedded at the core; services span Retail and Wholesale clients worldwide.
- Purpose of the section: overview of identified material impacts, risks and opportunities, how they link to strategy and the business model, and an explanation of the Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) methodology; references to related report sections for broader context.
- Value chain approach: DMA targets the most significant activities, products and services; scope extends beyond financial-statement consolidation to include own operations and indirect upstream/downstream relationships; six value-chain segments identified using internal data.
- Key sustainability nexus: the loan book is the primary driver of sustainability impacts; assessments are mainly at tier‑1 direct counterparties (e.g., financed corporates, retail clients), with tier‑2 considered for S2 (workers in the value chain) and S4 (consumers/end-users).
- Boundary choices: non-consolidated associates and joint ventures are treated as other business relationships and included in the DMA; intercompany transactions are excluded.
- Mapped value chain activities: 
  - Wholesale/Business/Retail Banking and Private Individuals: lending, deposits/savings, daily banking, trade finance, capital markets advisory, trading book, mortgages, insurance, investment and wealth-management products; product development, marketing, and distribution.
  - Own operations: supplier management, employee management, property management.
  - Treasury and investments: High Quality Liquid Assets, hedging, debt instruments, shareholder equity, and equity holdings.
- Principal actors covered: suppliers, employees, large corporates (incl. financial institutions), sovereigns/sub-sovereigns/agencies, self-employed/micro firms, SMEs/mid-corporates, private individual and private banking clients, corporate clients, and investee companies.
- Report context: excerpt from ING Group Annual Report 2024, Business model and strategy section.
text:
Our value chain
With a view to comprehensively captur e impacts, risks and opportunities, the DMA has to focus on the most 
significant activities, services and products. Therefore, the starting point of the DMA is understanding the 
structure of the bank’s business relationships and activities by identifying ING’s value-chain components.  
Since this assessment expands beyond the financial statement consolidation scope, we have assessed  our core business against our own operations and our (in)direct relationships in our upstream and/or 
downstream value chain . For our value chain identification, we have used internal data, which resulted in the 
identification of  six segments as depicted below.  
As a financial institution, our main business segment impacting  sustainability  matters is our loan book, 
through which we finance our clients and the economy. The assessment is mostly done at tier 1 direct 
contractual relationship-level (e.g. large corporates ING is financing; Retail customers ING is serving). The 
only exception is S2 ‘workers in the value chain’ and S4 ‘consumers and end-users’, where the assessment 
captures the bank’s direct counterparties’ (e.g. clients) social practices over tier 2 counterparties (i.e. with 
regards to affected workers in the value chain and end-users/consumers). Associates and joint ventures that 
are not consolidated in the financial statements are treated as the other business relationships, i.e. actors in 
the value chain (e.g. suppliers, investee companies), and as such are part of our DMA. Intercompany 
transactions are descoped  from our value chain for the DMA purpose.

title: Our double materiality assessment
heading: 2.2 Our double materiality assessment
start_phrase: This is the first year that we have performed our double materiality assessment in accordance with ESRS, based on the six identified value chain segments.
summary:
- First ESRS-aligned double materiality assessment, transitioning from prior GRI-based approach; key change is adding financial materiality to impact materiality.
- Materiality definitions:
  - Impact materiality (inside-out): actual or potential positive/negative impacts on people and the environment from financed activities, ING’s own operations, products, services, and business relationships.
  - Financial materiality (outside-in): risks and opportunities from environmental and societal changes affecting ING, notably via climate and environmental risk management.
- Time horizons used: very short (<1 year), short (1–3 years), medium (3–5 years), long (>5 years and at least 10), with ESRS requiring some forward-looking disclosures.
- Scope and evaluation: DMA based on six value chain segments; covers sector-agnostic topics E1–E5 (climate, pollution, water/marine resources, biodiversity/ecosystems, resource use/circular economy), S1–S4 (own workforce, workers in the value chain, affected communities, consumers/end-users), and G1 (business conduct), assessed for risk, opportunity, and double materiality with thresholds (Material, Important, Informative–Minimal).
- Outcomes: Despite methodology shift, topic-level results broadly consistent with prior year. S2 (Workers in the value chain) and S3 (Affected communities) not deemed material for ING’s value chains but still considered important.
- Salient human rights issues:
  - As lender to corporates: forced labour, child labour, land and resource-related community issues.
  - As procurer: occupational health and safety, modern slavery and forced labour.
  - Identification, management, and mitigation detailed in ING’s latest human rights report (ing.com).
text:
Our double materiality assessment
This is the first year that we have  performed our double materiality assessment in accordance with ESRS, 
based on the six identified value chain segments.  In the previous reporting periods, we based our materiality 
assessment on the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) reporting framework. The main change to the materiality 
assessment is the introduction of the ‘double’ materiality concept. Where GRI requires a look at impact 
materiality only, ESRS also requires a look at financial materiality.
A sustainability matter is deemed material when it meets the criteria for impact materiality, financial 
materiality, or both. The perspectives of materiality are defined as follows:
Impact materiality
Inside-out perspective
•Inside-out perspective is used to measure the actual or potential, 
positive or negative impacts on people or the environment.•As a financial institution, this refers to the business we finance, 
impacts caused or contributed to by ING and impacts which are 
directly linked to ING’s operations, products and services through 
its business relationships.
Financial materiality
Outside-in perspective
•Outside-in perspective is used to measure the risks and 
opportunities of a changing environment and society on ING.
•As a financial institution, it is especially mirrored in climate & 
environmental risk management.
A sustainability matter might be material in the very short, short , medium or long term, and as such is an 
essential component of the DMA. In defining our time horizons , we considered industry-specific guidance 
provided by the European Banking Authority (EBA) for the banking sector and combined these with the ESRS 
requirements:
•very short-term: less than 1 year;•short-term: between 1 and 3 years;
•medium-term: 3 to 5 years; and•long-term: over 5 years and at least 10 years.Although the A nnual  Report generally only contains information related to the current reporting year, ESRS 
sometimes requires us to disclose additional forward-looking information.

title: Process to identify impacts, risks and opportunities
heading: 2.3 Process to identify impacts, risks and opportunities
start_phrase: Via the double materiality assessment process, ING identifies impacts, risk s and opportunities across environmental, social and governance (ESG) sustainability matters, arising from its own operations or within the upstream or downstream value chain.
summary:
- Focus: Explains ING’s process for identifying impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) across its operations and value chain using a Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) aligned with ESRS.
- DMA governance and flow: Five-step approach—(1) identify activities and business relationships, (2) identify relevant sustainability matters, (3) execute the DMA, (4) validate results through stakeholder engagement, (5) obtain Management Board and Supervisory Board approval.
- Scoping methodology: Starts from balance sheet and P&L to pinpoint activities/assets subject to IROs; maps financial statement items to core business areas and portfolios; excludes portfolios with low likelihood of material IROs.
- Exposure classification: Categorizes assets and liabilities by characteristics such as loan/position maturity, counterparty type, product/service type, geography, industry, and collateral to understand where sustainability issues can materialize.
- Sustainability matters selection: Uses ESRS sector-agnostic inventory as the baseline for alignment and comparability; conducts market consultation and reviews past assessments to find entity-specific topics—none added; assesses topics across the full value chain, recognizing relevance varies by chain (details in the appendix).
- Assessment granularity: Evaluates all ESRS topics at sub-topic level; Social matters assessed at sub-sub-topic level; granularity set by internal and external data availability.
- Impact drivers: Defines and considers environmental (e.g., resource use, emissions), social (e.g., labor practices, human rights, equity, community health/safety), and governance (e.g., transparency, accountability, anti-corruption, compliance) drivers, with a forward-looking perspective.
- Risk drivers: Identifies ESG risks within existing risk categories, including transition and physical risks; accounts for forward-looking characteristics and dependencies on natural and human capital; links to broader ESG risk management.
- Opportunity drivers: Views opportunities as ESG-related conditions that can enhance the business model, strategy delivery, and value creation; prioritization aligned with publicly disclosed sustainability commitments.
text:
Via the  double materiality assessment process, ING identifies impacts, risk s and opportunities  across 
environmental, social and governance (ESG) sustainability matters, arising from its own operations or within 
the upstream or downstream value chain. The DMA is performed following a five-step approach:
Step 1 Identification of activities and business relationships
Step 2 Identification of relevant sustainability matters
Step 3 Execution of the double materiality assessment
Step 4 Validation of the outcome through stakeholders' engagement
Step 5 Approval by the management boards and Supervisory Board
Identification of activities and business relationships  
In determining the value chain segments and identifying which components are more likely to be associated 
with material IROs, ING uses the following three-step approach :
•Start from the balance sheet and profit and loss statements of the bank to identify activities and assets 
subject to impacts, risks and opportunities.
•Map the financial statement items to the core business areas and portfolios, mirroring ING’s internal 
organisation to ensure alignment with  sustainability steering . 
•Scope out the portfolios where a low likelihood of relevant IROs is expected.
The identification of assets, exposures and liabilities, subject to impacts and risks requires a classification of 
activities according to their characteristics to form  a view on how and where sustainability matters can 
materialise . In particular, the categori sation of exposures is performed on the basis of characteristics that 
include but are not limited to maturity of loan or position, counterparty type, type of activity/service/
product, geography, industry type or collateral type  as part of the DMA process.  ING’s value chain and its 
underlying portfolios are shown in the previous section under ‘ Business model and strategy ’.
Identif ication of relevant sustainability matters
The sector-agnostic inventory list of sustainability matters in ESRS is used as a starting point, to seek 
alignment with the ESRS disclosure requirements and comparability. In addition, we have assessed whether 
there are sustainability-related material IROs relevant to ING which are not yet covered by ESRS. This 
assessment consisted of market consultation to gather an understanding of the material matters of our 
peers and reflection on our own materiality assessment performed in previous reporting periods. The assessment resulted in no additional entity -specific disclosures . The topics within the sustainability matters 
are assessed for our full value chain. However, not all topics are relevant for all value chains. See ‘ Appendix to 
the Executive Board report ’ for an overview of the relevant sustainability matter s per value chain. 
ING determined the level of granularity at which the DMA should be conducted based on internal and 
external data availability.  All ESRS topics , except for Social , which is assessed at the sub-sub-topic level, are 
evaluated at the sub-topic leve l. ING developed an understanding of all relevant impact drivers as well as 
financial drivers with respect to sustainability matters.
Impacts  are recognised in a form of drivers causing changes in nature and anthropogenic1 asse ts, including 
quality of life. To ensure a holistic approach, a diverse range of factors across environmental, social and 
governance dimensions were addressed and, where possible, their forward-looking nature: 
•Environmental impact drivers relate to the quantity of a natural resource that is (used as) an input or 
non-product output of a business activity e.g. emissions related to manufacturing facilities. These drivers 
stem from changes in quantity or quality of the natural capital that occur as a consequence of an impact 
driver.
•Social impact drivers refer to factors that affect the wellbeing, rights, and social conditions of individuals 
and communities. Examples include labour practices, human rights, and social equity. The social impact 
drivers highlight changes such as improved or deteriorated living conditions, social inclusion or exclusion, 
and shifts in community health and safety. •Governance impact drivers relate to factors that influence the governance structures, practices and 
ethical standards of an organi sation. These drivers include corporate governance practices, transparency, 
accountability, anti-corruption measures, and compliance with laws and regulations. They affect an 
organisation’s ethical standing, regulatory compliance, and overall governance quality . 
Risks  are identified by drivers that materialise in existing risk categories and distinguish between the various 
types of ESG risks, such as transition and physical risks in the case of environmental matters.  ING accounts 
for the full spectrum of ESG risk drivers, considering their distinctive characteristics, such as their forward-
looking nature or where risks stem from the impact or dependencies on nature and human capital. For more 
information on how ESG risk s are integrated in the overall risk management process, see the ‘ ESG Risk’ 
section .
Opportunities  are understood as potential environmental, social or governance events or conditions that 
could materially enhance ING’s business model or ability to achieve strategic goals and create value, and 
may therefore influence decisions – both internally and externally. The identification of opportunities is 
driven by ING’s publicly disclosed sustainability commitments where the opportunity is currently explicitly 
pursued. Contents ING at a glance Strategy, business model

title: Execution of the double materiality assessment
heading: 2.4 Execution of the double materiality assessment
start_phrase: The DMA leverages on renowned external data sources , internal data, voluntary reports and other regulatory disclosures to assess the impact from ING’s own operations and upstream and downstream value chain .
summary:
- Explains how ING executes its Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) across its full value chain (own operations, upstream, downstream) using a “gross” approach that excludes mitigating actions.
- Identifies data foundations: renowned external sources, internal data, voluntary reports, and regulatory disclosures; combines quantitative and qualitative methods against predefined thresholds.
- Defines impact materiality via severity (scale, scope, irremediability) and likelihood across time horizons for both actual and potential positive/negative impacts.
- Defines financial materiality via magnitude and likelihood arising from impacts, dependencies, and context analyses; considers dependencies on natural, human, and social resources, business relationships, and reputation; supplements indicators with expert judgment.
- Details risk assessment: mirrors approach for negative impacts and dependencies; incorporates individual exposures and context; determines portfolio risk materiality as the maximum across dimensions; enhanced by internal data and scenario analyses.
- Details opportunity assessment: evaluates magnitude (financial and non-financial gains, e.g., cost savings) across “use of own resources” and “reliance on relationships” dimensions; likelihood tied to time horizon.
- Describes scoring framework: combined scores from 1 (minimal) to 5 (critical) using a conversion matrix of severity/magnitude versus likelihood; sustainability matters are material if rated “critical” or “significant.”
- References “Technical notes to the double materiality assessment” for further methodological details and value-chain-specific sustainability matters.
text:
Execution of the double  materiality assessment
The DMA leverages on renowned  external data sources , internal data, voluntary reports and other regulatory 
disclosures to assess the impact from ING’s own operations and upstream and downstream value chain . 
To determine materiality, ING leverages on a number of quantitative and qualitative approaches to assess 
the level of the impacts and potential risks and opportunities a gainst predetermined materiality thresholds . 
Assessment of materiality follows a  'gross'  approach, meaning without taking  mitigating actions , initiated by 
ING, into account. The materiality of sustainability topics is determined for our full value chain1, following the 
approach illustrated and summarised below. 
Impact mater iality,  for both actual and potential (positive and negative) impacts, is informed  by the severity  
of the impact and combined with the likelihood that it results in the potential impact. Severity is determined 
by scale (how grave or beneficial the impact is), scope (how widespread the impact is), and irremediable 
character (to what extent the negative impacts could be remediated). Likelihood captures the likelihood of 
materialisation of the underlying impact for all time horizons . Financial materiality  is assessed based on a combination of magnitude and likelihood, stemming from 
impacts, dependencies, or context analyses. An impact may be financially material from inception or 
become financially material over time as identified throug h im pact materiality. Dependencies on natural, 
human, and social resources are considered based on their influence on ING’s ability to access and utilise 
these resources affecting their quality and pricing. Context analyses include ING’s dependencies on business 
relationships and reputational risks or gains, viewed collectively for financial materiality. Indicators from 
internal or external data are supplemented by expert judgement from sector or risk specialists.
For risks, the approach to dependencies is similar to the appro ach for negative impacts. Once the 
assessment of the dependencies and negative impacts is performed , a view of individual exposures and 
context analysis is considered. ING assesses the risk materiality in a view of the value chains’ portfolio, as the 
maximum  across the three dimensions  (max of negative impact and context analyses) . Wher e possible, the 
assessment is enhanced by the use of internal data sources and scenario analyses. See ‘ Technical notes to 
the double materiality assessment ’ for more details on the approach.
For opportunities, magnitude reflects financial and non-financial implications potenti ally leading to gains or 
decreased costs, such as energy costs. This assessment has been performed across the ‘use of own 
resources’ (extent to which ING uses its resources to pursue a specific opportunity as a result of a certain 
sustainability matter evolution) and ‘r eliance on relationship ’ (potential reputational and financial gains from 
meeting commitments and adapting ESG standards, while attracting investors and clients looking for 
credible sustainable investment options) dimensions . The likelihood reflects the time horizon as described 
above. These assessments result  in combined  scores ranging from minimal (1 = very low) to critical (5 = very 
high).  Each combined score is assessed using the conversion matrix below, where a sustainability matter is 
deemed material if it scores as ‘critical’ or ‘significant’.

title: Validation of the outcome through stakeholders’ engagement
heading: 2.5 Validation of the outcome through stakeholders’ engagement
start_phrase: To validate the outcome of our double materiality assessment, we engaged with our key stakeholders.
summary: The excerpt outlines how ING validated the results of its double materiality assessment (DMA) through structured engagement with two stakeholder groups—affected stakeholders and users. It describes a standardized process of workshops, surveys, and in-depth interviews to review the DMA methodology, preliminary results, completeness, and different time horizons, with interview minutes confirmed to ensure accuracy. Where direct engagement was not feasible, proxies were used (e.g., NGOs for affected communities and nature; internal and public data for retail customers). Stakeholder feedback was evaluated systematically for recurrence, consistency, evidentiary support, and relevance, with references cross-checked and discussed with subject-matter experts. An example is provided where some stakeholders expected “Workers in the value chain (S2)” and “Affected communities (S3)” to be material; ING maintained their non-material status given limited portfolio exposure to high human-rights-risk sectors, while continuing to report on them as salient human rights issues. The text also details stakeholder-specific engagement channels and focus areas: employees (S1, G1), customers and investors (all ESRS topics), and society via NGOs and regulatory experts (E1–E5, S2–S4, and all ESRS topics for governments/regulators). Finally, it records governance approvals: methodology endorsed by the ESG Risk Committee and the DMA outcome approved by the management boards and Supervisory Board, following communication to internal stakeholders and value-chain owners.
text:
To validate the outcome of our double materiality assessment, we engaged with our key stakeholders. We 
asked  them or their representatives to validate  our identified material IROs , where validation refers to 
whether our stakeholders recognise the outcome or are missing a topic.  We identified two main stakeholder 
groups: affected stakeholders  and users, hereafter collectively referred to as ‘stakeholders’. 
Per stakeholder group, sessions were organised to discuss ING’s DMA methodology and preliminary results, 
to answer questions and collect feedback. The stakeholders shared their views through surveys or in-depth 
interviews . The sessions were conducted by our stakeholder engagement team and subject-matter experts, 
according to a standardised approach, presenting predefined questions on the soundness of preliminary 
r e s u l t s ,  c o m p l e t e n e s s  a n d  d i f f e r e n t  t i m e - h o r i z o n  p e r s p e c t i v e s .   I n  t h e  c a s e  o f  i n t e r v i e w s ,  t h e  minutes were 
confirmed with the stakeholders following the meetings to ensure a common understanding and accurate 
interpretation of the discussion.
Proxies were used to cover the views of stakeholders when direct engagement was not feasible. For instance, 
NGOs were invited to represent affected communities and silent stakeholders like nature and biodiversity. 
For our private customers, the evaluation of internal and publicly available data has been used to cover their  
views. The right side of this page summarises our key stakeholders and how the engagement took place.
Stakeholders  reviewed our approach, evaluating the suitability of the data used and assessing the 
significance and scale of the results. We carefully analysed the feedback provided, considering factors such 
as recurrence, consistency, strength, supporting evidence, and relevance of the arguments. In interpreting 
the feedback, we looked for patterns, such as similar feedback from different stakeholder groups or repeated 
comments. Additionally, we prioritised fact-driven substantiation. References were cross-checked with 
credible sources and discussed with subject-matter experts.
An example of  stakeholder engagement was the expectation, of certain stakeholders, that Workers in the 
value chain (S2) and Affected communities (S3) would be concluded as material, given the importance of  
these topics in our due diligence process and policies guided by international standards and guidelines. 
However, after carefully considering this feedback, we decided not to change the DMA outcome, as ING h as 
limited exposure  to sectors vulnerable to human rights issues1. We recognise the importance  of these  topics 
as salient human rights  issues and  will continue to report on them in our human rights report .

title: Approval by the management boards and Supervisory Board
heading: 2.6 Approval by the management boards and Supervisory Board
start_phrase: The outcome of the DMA was communicated to all relevant stakeholders and value-chain segment owners.
summary:
- Purpose: Validate the double materiality assessment (DMA) outcomes and identified material impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) with stakeholders, checking recognition and any missing topics.
- Stakeholder scope and methods: Two groups—affected stakeholders and users—engaged via sessions, surveys, and in-depth interviews. A standardized approach covered soundness, completeness, and different time horizons. Interview minutes were confirmed to ensure accurate interpretation.
- Use of proxies: NGOs represented affected communities and silent stakeholders such as nature and biodiversity; internal and public data represented private customers; ING experts covered supervisory/public/regulatory perspectives when direct engagement was not possible.
- Feedback evaluation: Inputs were analyzed for recurrence, consistency, strength, evidence, and relevance; patterns across groups were identified; fact-based substantiation was prioritized and cross-checked with credible sources and subject-matter experts.
- Example outcome: Despite some stakeholder expectations for Workers in the value chain (S2) and Affected communities (S3) to be material, ING maintained its DMA outcome due to limited exposure to human rights–vulnerable sectors, while continuing to report on these salient issues in the human rights report.
- Governance and approvals: DMA methodology approved by the ESG Risk Committee; outcomes approved by the management boards and the Supervisory Board, after communication to relevant stakeholders and value-chain owners.
- Engagement by stakeholder segment:
  - Our people: Direct workshops with employees; proxies via European/local works councils; feedback via surveys and interviews; focus on S1 and G1.
  - Our customers: Retail via proxies (customer complaints, consumer protection publications); Business and Wholesale via proxies (sessions with ING sector experts); focus on all ESRS topics.
  - Investors: Direct sessions with investors and associations; focus on all ESRS topics.
  - Society: Direct sessions with NGOs as proxies for nature, biodiversity, climate, and workers in the value chain; proxy sessions with ING regulatory/public affairs experts; focus on E1–E5, S2–S4, and all ESRS topics for governments and regulators.

title: Internal controls over sustainability reporting
heading: 2.8 Internal controls over sustainability reporting
start_phrase: At ING we have integrated our sustainability-related risk management and internal controls into our existing Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework and three-lines-of-defence model.
summary:
- Scope and standards: ING reports on material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) in line with ESRS disclosure and application requirements. For the 2024 Sustainability Statement, ING includes applicable mandatory, relevant and material information, while omitting certain requirements not applicable in the first reporting years. A Reference index provides details.

- Governance and controls: Sustainability-related risk management and internal controls are integrated into ING’s Enterprise Risk Management framework and three-lines-of-defence model, aligned with the annual integrated reporting and CSRD governance. ING acknowledges risk of material misstatement (e.g., human error, third-party controls, fraud) and has implemented mitigating measures.

- IRO overview table: Presents where IROs arise across the value chain (upstream, own operations, downstream), the time horizons (very short to long term), and which business models are affected (Private Individuals, Private Banking, Wholesale Banking, Business Banking).

- Environmental
  - Climate change (E1)
    - Negative impact: financing high-emitting sectors and non–energy-efficient properties.
    - Risks: potential (non)financial losses from transition risks (defaults, reduced collateral values) and physical risks (storms, floods, sea-level rise, temperature increases).
    - Opportunities: ING’s voluntary commitments to support clients’ climate transition.
    - Broadly spans the value chain, multiple time horizons; affects Private Individuals, Private Banking, Wholesale Banking, Business Banking.
  - Biodiversity (E4)
    - Negative impact: lending to clients whose operations cause irreversible harm to species.
    - Risks: reputational and financial losses tied to severity of impacts.
    - Primarily linked to Wholesale Banking.

- Social
  - Own workforce (S1)
    - Negative impacts: unrealistic workloads, gender inequality, pay gaps, inadequate prevention of violence and harassment—affecting wellbeing, especially for vulnerable groups.
    - Positive impacts: upskilling, new competencies, diverse teams.
    - Risks: reputational and turnover risks; risks related to disability inclusion and workplace accessibility.
    - Located in own operations; relevant across time horizons.
  - Consumers and end-users (S4)
    - Negative impacts: insufficient access to quality information, lack of social inclusion, inadequate privacy protection—potentially harming customer wellbeing.
    - Risks: financial losses, regulatory exposure, reputational harm.
    - Applies to Private Individuals and Private Banking; primarily downstream; spans multiple time horizons.

- Governance
  - Business conduct (G1)
    - Risks: financial loss, regulatory fines, and reputational damage from breaches of corporate culture, bribery and corruption, and failure to protect whistleblowers.
    - Located in own operations; relevant across time horizons.
text:
Internal controls over sustainability reporting
At ING we have integrated our sustainability-related risk management and internal controls into our existing 
Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework and three-lines-of-defence model. See our ‘ Risk management 
framework ’ for more information. With this approach we aim to strengthen the governance and controls 
over sustainability disclosures, aligning them with financial and non-financial risk oversight.
The process for preparing the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) sustainability statement is 
aligned with the annual integrated reporting process and governance. The information in ING’s 
Sustainability Statement is inherently subject to the risk of material misstatement, for example due to 
human error, inadequate controls including in respect of third parties and/or fraud. ING has therefore 
implemented several mitigating measures to manage identified risks.Contents ING at a glance Strategy, business model

title: Our sustainability governance - Introduction
heading: 3 Our sustainability governance
start_phrase: At ING, we have integrated sustainability into our existing governance.
summary:
Our sustainability governance
At ING, we have integrated sustainability into our existing governance. For details about the full function of 
governance bodies and the composition of our Supervisory Board (SB), Executive Board (EB), and 
Management Board Banking (MBB) , including their roles, expertise, and remuneration, see the ‘ Our 
leadership and corporate governance ’ section.  The remainder of this section wi ll elaborate on the

text:
Our sustainability governance
At ING, we have integrated sustainability into our existing governance. For details about the full function of 
governance bodies and the composition of our Supervisory Board (SB), Executive Board (EB), and 
Management Board Banking (MBB) , including their roles, expertise, and remuneration, see the ‘ Our 
leadership and corporate governance ’ section.  The remainder of this section wi ll elaborate on the 
governance around sustainability .

title: The Supervisory Board
heading: 3.1 The Supervisory Board
start_phrase: In 2022, we established an ad hoc ESG committee assisting the SB with regards to matters relating to ESG, including, but not limited to, the development and integration of ESG across the company and its strategy, and the ratification/ discussion/ adoption of new and updated key policies, among others, related to business conduct.
summary:
- Sustainability is integrated into ING’s overall governance; detailed roles and compositions of SB, EB, and MBB are in the leadership and corporate governance section, while this section focuses on sustainability governance.
- Supervisory Board: An ESG Committee, created ad hoc in 2022, became a permanent committee in 2024; meets quarterly; includes at least one member from each other SB committee; convenes jointly with the Audit Committee when disclosure or control topics are discussed.
- Management boards (EB and MBB): ESG is a standing agenda item in weekly meetings; ESG risks, impacts, opportunities, and strategy are embedded across discussions; boards frequently decide on ESG-related topics and approve key policies, including those related to business conduct.
- Senior management governance:
  - ESG Risk Committee: Ensures execution of ESG risk matters from the SB; acts as a technical adviser; aligns functional and business issues; plans ESG risk priorities; advises on approval of material ESG risk items.
  - Disclosure Committee: Senior management, business, and risk representatives advise the boards on disclosure obligations; reviews external presentations, including sustainability information, before public release.
- Business governance:
  - Wholesale Banking: A Sustainability Steering Committee (since 2022) assigns ownership and resources, owns ESG KPIs, and sets WB sustainability strategy, including sector targets and sector-based transition plans.
  - Retail Banking (Private Individuals, Business Banking, Private Banking): Governance via councils (e.g., Net Zero Housing Committee, Business Banking ESG Council) steering sustainable product development and lending portfolio progress toward climate goals; responsibilities cascade to experts and country teams; country sustainability leads have a functional line to the global head of Sustainability to link global and local activities.
text:
The Supervisory Board 
In 2022, we established an ad hoc ESG committee assisting the SB with regards to matters relating to ESG, 
including, but not limited to, the development and integration of ESG across the company and its strategy, 
and the ratification/ discussion/ adoption of new and updated key policies, among others, related to business 
conduct.
During 2024, given the dynamic and continuously evolving nature of ESG, t he ESG committee  was 
established as a permanent committee. The ESG Committee meets on a quarterly basis and consists of at 
least one member of each of the other committees. When disclosure or controls topics are on the agenda, 
the ESG Committee is always combined with the A udit Committee (AC) .

title: The management boards
heading: 3.2 The management boards
start_phrase: ESG is a regular subject on the agenda of ING’s management boards (the EB and the MBB) , in their capacity of day-to-day management of the business and as part of their responsibility for ING’s long-term (ESG) strategy .
summary:
- ING integrates sustainability into its overall governance, with detailed roles and structures described in a separate corporate governance section; this section focuses on sustainability-specific governance.
- Supervisory Board (SB) oversight includes an ESG Committee, set up ad hoc in 2022 and made permanent in 2024; it meets quarterly, includes at least one member from each other SB committee, and convenes jointly with the Audit Committee when disclosure or controls are discussed.

The management  boards
ESG is a regular subject on the agenda of ING’s management boards (the EB and the MBB) , in their capacity 
of day-to-day management of the business and as part of their responsibility for ING’s long-term (ESG) 
strategy . ESG-related matters, the related impacts, risks and opportunities and their effect on our strategy 
are intertwined in many other discussions and topics discussed by the EB and the MBB. These meetings 
generally take place on a weekly basis.
As we take steps to further integrate and embed climate  and other ESG actions into the business, many of

means that the management boards  are discussing and taking decisions on ESG-related topics on a frequent 
basis. This includes the review and approval of new and updated key policies, among others, related to 
business conduct. More information on the role of the EB and MBB is described in the relevant charter on

summary:

Our climate is changing due to the release of greenhouse gas  (GHG) emissions into the atmosphere. Our

helping to drive down emissions to meet the global goal of net zero by 2050; building up the financing of the 
new technologies and sustainable systems of the future; and finding ways to enable people to play their part

text:
Climate change
Our climate is changing due to the release of greenhouse gas  (GHG) emissions into the atmosphere. Our 
climate action activities are focused on the three areas where we believe we can make the greatest impact: 
helping to drive down emissions to meet the global goal of net zero by 2050; building up the financing of the 
new technologies and sustainable systems of the future; and finding ways to enable people to play their part 
in the transition. For ING, climate adaptation is essential to reduce vulnerability against the physical impact 
of climate change. We work on reducing those risks by financing the required adaptation of our clients and 
communities .

title: Identified impacts, risks and opportunities
heading: 4.1.1 Identified impacts, risks and opportunities
start_phrase: This section elaborates on the material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) associated with climate change, and how these factors interact with and influence ING’s strategy and business model.
summary:
- Focus and goals: ING addresses climate change by targeting three impact areas—reducing emissions to align with net zero by 2050, scaling finance for new low‑carbon technologies and sustainable systems, and enabling people to contribute to the transition—while emphasizing climate adaptation to lower vulnerability to physical climate impacts by financing client and community resilience measures.

- Material IROs and scope: Climate change mitigation and adaptation are deemed material across Wholesale Banking (WB), Business Banking (BB), and Private Individuals (PI) real estate lending. A sector transition plan prioritizes the most carbon‑intensive sectors and is complemented by policies and guidelines that manage negative impacts, risks, and create opportunities.

- Mitigation: 
  - Negative impacts: Emissions linked to lending in high‑emitting sectors; and, in real estate, properties with poor energy performance, assessed using the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD).
  - Risks (transition risk): For WB/BB, costs from adopting low‑carbon technologies and exposure to carbon pricing (including indirect emissions); for real estate, energy price changes and EPBD IV effects on customer income, repayment capacity, and renovation financing eligibility. Non‑compliance can lead to reputational, legal/regulatory, and financial consequences.
  - Opportunities: Growth aligned with public commitments—mobilizing more WB volumes for the transition, issuing green funding, and advancing the Terra approach via increased renewable financing.

- Adaptation:
  - Definition and linkage: Adjusting to actual/anticipated climate impacts; closely tied to managing physical risk.
  - Physical risks: Acute (storms, floods) and chronic (rising sea levels and temperatures) hazards that heighten default risk and non‑performing loans through multiple transmission channels, creating financial vulnerabilities for ING.
text:
This section elaborates on the material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs)  associated with climate 
change, and how these factors interact with and influence ING’s strategy and business model. Climate 
change mitigation and climate change adaptation are concluded material for our Wholesale Banking (WB)  
and Business Banking (BB) value chains, and for our Private Individuals (PI) value chain (real estate lending).
The IROs,  as further explained in this section, are managed in several ways by ING. We start by explaining 
our sector transition plan, which focuses on transitioning the most carbon-intensive sectors towards net 
zero, followed by other policies and guidelines we have in place. Where our sector transition plan mainly 
addresses our negative impacts and risks, it can also create opportunities. With our other policies and 
guidelines, we address our negative impacts and risks, as well as our opportunities.

title: Climate change mitigation
heading: 4.1.2 Climate change mitigation
start_phrase: Climate change mitigation refers to the process of reducing GHG emissions and holding the increase in the global average temperature to 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels, in line with the ambition of the Paris Agreement1.
summary:
- Focus and scope: ING’s climate strategy centers on mitigating and adapting to climate change across Wholesale Banking, Business Banking, and Private Individuals (real estate lending), with a goal aligned to net zero by 2050.
- Three climate action pillars: 1) drive down emissions, 2) finance new low‑carbon technologies and sustainable systems, and 3) enable people to participate in the transition; adaptation financing is emphasized to reduce physical climate vulnerability.
- Management approach: A sector transition plan targets the most carbon‑intensive sectors, complemented by policies and guidelines that address negative impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Mitigation: Defined as reducing GHG emissions to limit warming to 1.5°C (Paris Agreement). Key negative impacts arise from lending to high‑emitting sectors and to real estate with poor energy performance (assessed against EPBD).
- Transition risks: For corporates, costs of new technologies/retrofits and carbon pricing on indirect emissions; for real estate, energy price changes and EPBD IV effects on income, payment behavior, and renovation financing eligibility; plus compliance risks (reputational, legal/regulatory, financial).
- Opportunities: Scaling climate transition financing via increased Wholesale Banking volumes mobilised, green funding frameworks, the Terra approach, and expanded renewable financing ambitions.
- Adaptation and physical risk: Defined as adjusting to actual/expected impacts; physical risks stem from acute events (storms, floods) and chronic trends (sea-level rise, temperature increases), raising default and non-performing loan risks through multiple transmission channels.
- Materiality: Climate mitigation and adaptation are material topics across ING’s key value chains and influence strategy and the business model.
text:
Climate change mitigation refers to the process of reducing GHG  emissions and holding the increase in the 
global average temperature to 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels,  in line with the ambition of the Paris 
Agreement1.
Negative impact on climate change is a result of lending to the most carbon-intensive sectors via our 
lending book. Emissions from these sectors might lead to an increase in average temperatures and 
potentially to more extreme weather events over the long term, unless companies and properties effectively 
transition to becoming net zero.  For our lending book , we have identified the following negative impacts: •Wholesale  and Business Banking lending: N egative impact arises from financing  operations/projects in 
high emitting sectors. 
•Real estate lending: Properties with poor energy performance are considered a high negative impact in 
the short and medium term, where all non net-zero properties are associated with a material negative 
impact in the long term. Assessment of negative impact relies o n the Energy Performance Building 
Directive (EPBD).
Risks  on climate change mitigation materialise  in the form of transition risk , which can lead to financial 
challenges for ING’s clients and potential losses for ING through customer defaults and reduced collateral 
values. For our lending book, we have identified the following potential financial risks: 
•Wholesale and Business Banking lending: Transition risk for high-emitting companies can arise from 
efforts to reduce GHG emissions through the adoption of new technologies and retrofits, as well as from 
the additional costs associated with carbon pricing for indirect emissions.•Real estate lending : Change in energy prices and EPBD IV implementation c an have a negative impact on 
customer income, payment discipline, and eligibility for property renovation financing. 
Additionally, failing to comply with applicable laws and regulations, and the inability to mitigate this risk, 
may result in reputational damage, legal and regulatory sanctions, and/or financial loss.
Opportunities  are identified in alignment with ING’s  publicly disclosed voluntary commitments to support  
the climate transition, such as our aim to increase our Wholesale Banking volumes mobilised, our ambition 
to fund the transition to a low-carbon economy via our green funding framework and our Terra approach 
through our renewable financing ambition.

title: Climate change adaptation
heading: 4.1.3 Climate change adaptation
start_phrase: Climate change adaptation refers to the process of adjusting to actual and anticipated climate change and its impacts.
summary:
- Focus and strategy: ING targets three climate action priorities—driving emissions down toward net zero by 2050, scaling financing for new low‑carbon technologies and sustainable systems, and enabling customers to participate in the transition—while prioritizing climate adaptation to reduce vulnerability to physical impacts by financing client and community resilience.
- Scope of impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs): Climate change mitigation and adaptation are material across Wholesale Banking (WB), Business Banking (BB), and Private Individuals (PI; real estate lending). ING manages IROs via a sector transition plan for carbon‑intensive sectors, complemented by policies and guidelines that address both risks and opportunities.
- Mitigation—negative impacts: Lending to high‑emitting sectors and to low‑efficiency real estate increases GHG emissions and long‑term temperature rise risk; poor energy performance properties are high impact in the short/medium term and all non‑net‑zero properties in the long term (assessed via EPBD).
- Mitigation—risks: Transition risk for corporates arises from decarbonization costs (technology upgrades, retrofits, indirect supplier costs) and carbon pricing; for real estate, energy price changes and EPBD IV implementation may strain borrower income, payment behavior, and renovation financing eligibility. Non‑compliance may trigger reputational, legal, regulatory, and financial consequences.
- Mitigation—opportunities: ING aims to expand sustainable finance through increased WB mobilized volumes, green funding frameworks, the Terra approach, and renewable financing ambitions.
- Adaptation—physical risks: Acute events (storms, floods) and chronic shifts (sea level rise, temperature increases) can cause defaults and losses.
  - Residential real estate: Asset damage, devaluations, insurance availability constraints, and borrower income impairment after disasters.
  - Wholesale/Business Banking: Infrastructure damage, operational interruptions, cost increases, revenue declines, supply disruptions, higher insurance costs, and third‑party claims affect borrower profitability and repayment capacity.
  - Governments/sovereigns: Lower tax revenues and higher spending for disaster response/adaptation can raise borrowing costs and restrict market access.
- Financial effects and resilience:
  - Current effects: Climate risk not yet fully embedded in IFRS 9 ECL due to data gaps; 2024 steps include explicit climate risk drivers in provisioning. Physical risk effects are based on actual events (e.g., Spain provision for payment holidays after Valencia floods). Transition risk captured via a management adjustment to ECL for current corporate portfolios.
  - Anticipated effects: Disclosures aligned with phased‑in EBA Pillar III ESG templates—Template 5 (physical risk exposures) and Template 2 (real estate energy efficiency)—with scope and resilience analysis in the appendix.
  - Risk controls: For material physical risks, mandatory credit risk mitigations (insurance or alternatives), enhanced underwriting data on adaptation, controlled financing amounts, or asset rejection if unmitigated; real estate valuations must reflect jurisdiction‑specific hazards.
- View on transition risk and stranded assets: High‑emitting sector exposure does not automatically imply default; structured transition planning and robust risk management can enable viable transformation. A three‑year horizon is too short to attribute defaults solely to transition failure; classifying all high‑carbon exposures as stranded over longer horizons is overly conservative. Bottom‑up transition risk assessment remains challenging due to data and forecasting limits.
- Real estate transition uncertainty: EPBD IV transposition into national law is expected by May 2026, creating interim uncertainty in linking EPC/primary energy demand to transition risk; sector transition plans for commercial and residential real estate are in place.
- Overall coverage: ING considers mid‑term transition risk significantly addressed through its Terra approach, which covers most emissions‑intensive sectors in the WB loan book.
text:
Climate change adaptation refers to the process of adjusting to actual and anticipated climate change and 
its impacts. It is intrinsically linked to physical risk, as it involves implementing strategies to manage and 
mitigate the effects of climate-related physical events.
Physical risks  can arise from acute , event-driven occurrences, such as storms and floods, as well as from 
chronic, long-term shifts and trends, like rising sea levels and temperatures. These risks increase the 
likelihood of defaults and non-performing loans, exposing ING to financial vulnerabilities through various 
transmission channels, including but not limited to:Contents ING at a glance Strategy, business model

devaluations, early retirement of existing assets, and a potential reduction in the availability of 
insurance for assets in high-risk locations.
•Impairment of borrowers’ abilities to service their loan payments, as well as eligibility for property 
renovation financing due to financial distress caused by natural disasters.•Wholesale and Business Banking lending: I nfrastructure damage, operational interruptions, increased 
operating costs, reduced revenue due to fall in customers demand, impact on the availability of raw 
materials, damage to production facilities, claims from third parties and higher insurance costs may 
result in unexpected expenses and significant losses. Consequently, this can lead to reductions in income 
and profits for borrowers, affecting their ability to repay loans. The loss of income and higher insurance 
premiums may increase the risk of client default.
•Governments : Income effects from physical risk events may primarily arise through tax and spending 
channels. Lower tax revenues may result from impaired corporates, reduced household income, and an 
overall reduction in output. Higher government spending is likely to take place to address – and partly 
compensate for – negative economic impacts, and cover adaptation costs. As a result, sovereigns, 
including subnational institutions, could be confronted with higher borrowing costs or limited access to 
debt markets.

title: Financial effects and resilience of ING’s strategy and business model
heading: 4.1.4 Financial effects and resilience of ING’s strategy and business model
start_phrase: For the identified risks we have two approaches to determine our current financial effects, more explicitly for physical risk and transition risk.
summary:
- Physical risk impacts by segment:
  - Residential real estate: extreme events can cause write-offs, asset devaluations, early retirements, reduced insurance availability; borrower distress may impair loan servicing and renovation financing.
  - Wholesale/Business Banking: infrastructure damage, operational interruptions, higher costs, reduced demand, supply issues, facility damage, third-party claims, and rising insurance premiums can depress income and increase default risk.
  - Governments: lower tax revenues and higher spending from disaster response/adaptation may raise borrowing costs or restrict market access.

- Financial effects and resilience:
  - Two approaches to quantify climate impacts: event-based provisioning for physical risk and a management adjustment for transition-risk ECLs.
  - IFRS 9 ECL models cannot yet fully isolate climate risk due to limited data, though 2024 enhancements add climate-risk drivers.
  - Example: 2024 provision in Spain for payment holidays after severe floods in Valencia.
  - Disclosures follow phased EBA Pillar III ESG: Template 5 (physical risk exposures) and Template 2 (real estate energy efficiency).
  - Proactive risk management: mandatory mitigations (insurance/adaptation), enhanced underwriting data, controlled financing, or asset rejection; material hazards embedded in real estate valuations.

- Transition risk perspective:
  - Arises from policy, technology, and market shifts; high-emitting sectors face capex and indirect supplier costs, and potential demand decline.
  - Not all high-emitting sectors will default; caution against labeling all exposures as stranded, especially over short horizons; bottom-up assessments remain challenging.
  - Real estate efficiency upgrades are a component of transition risk, with regulatory uncertainty pending EPBD IV transposition (expected May 2026).
  - Mid-term transition risk largely addressed via the Terra approach across emissions-intense sectors.

- Climate stress testing:
  - ING’s climate stress-test extends existing ICAAP/EBA frameworks with overlays for transition and physical risks on corporate and mortgage credit portfolios.

- Opportunities and commitments:
  - Support clients’ sustainable transition through products and green funding.
  - Financial effects tracked via progress against public commitments (e.g., Terra transition plan for renewable power, mobilized volumes, green funding framework).

- Transition plan and Terra approach:
  - Sustainability is core to strategy; aim to steer the most carbon-intensive portfolio segments toward climate goals.
  - Terra measures client emission intensities against sector decarbonization pathways; upstream oil & gas steered on financial exposure.
  - Collection of Client Transition Plans in Wholesale Banking to deepen sector plans and guide client engagement, advisory, and financing.
  - Monitoring absolute financed emissions enables hotspot analyses and informs expansion of the Terra scope.
text:
For the identified risks we have two approaches to determine our current financial effects, more explicitly for 
physical risk and transition risk. Currently, it is not yet possible to fully incorporate climate risk separately 
into IFRS 9 ECL models given the lack of sufficient empirical historical data and data limitations in the risk 
assessments on client level. However, ING has taken next steps in 2024 to more explicitly cover for climate-
risk drivers in loan loss provisioning. See our ‘ Risk Management – credit risk ’ section regarding loan loss 
provisioning for mor e information.
•For physical risk, we base our current financial effects on actual events that took place during the 
reporting year. In 2024, a provision was recognised in Spain due to payment holidays provided for 
customers with collateral or activities in the areas impacted by the severe floods in the Valencia area .•For transition risk, we updated our provisions methodology applying a management adjustment, 
capturing the expected credit losses of our current business client  portfolio.
For the anticipated financial effects, ING is making use of the phased-in requirements and only discloses the 
EBA Pillar III ESG information where applicable and compatible with the ESRS. Template 5 is used to provide 
insights on the consolidated level of sensitive exposures to physical risk and template 2 provides insights into 
our real estate portfolio and the energy efficiency of the related collaterals – both templates are included in 
the ‘ Appendix to the Executive Board report ’ together with the scope of our resilience analysis.With regards to the exposures to physical risk, ING takes a proactive approach in managing and monitoring 
the identified risk. Lending criteria on material physical risk requires mandatory credit risk mitigations, either 
through insurance or alternative credit risk mitigations. These include collecting additional data during the 
underwriting process proving risk adaptation, controlling financed amount or even rejecting the asset where 
neither physical risk can be proven or other mitigation  can be applied. For commercial  and residential real 
estate assets it is mandatory to have material hazards (by jurisdiction) incorporated in the current market 
value of the property.
Transition risk refers to an institution’s financial loss that can result, directly or indirectly, from the process of 
adjustment towards a lower-carbon and more environmentally sustainable economy. This could be 
triggered by a relatively abrupt adoption of climate and environmental policies , technological progress or 
changes in market sentiment and preferences. Sectors with high GHG emissions will likely incur significant 
capital expenditures during the decarbonisation process, along with additional indirect costs from their 
suppliers’ decarbonisation efforts. Demand for carbon-intensive products and technologies may also 
contract. 
Being part of a high-emitting sector does not necessarily mean inevitable default in a decarbonisation 
scenario. Adhering to regulatory expectations for structured transition planning and avoiding the 
stigmatisation of economic sectors, combined with sound risk management practices, suggests that these 
sectors might not disappear entirely. We believe that some of the best companies within these sectors could 
successfully transform. The general logic of ESRS suggests that material transition risk is closely tied to assets 
that could become stranded in a rapid decarbonisation scenario. For banks, this primarily means defaulted 
loans. We believe that a three-year period is too short to account for defaults caused solely by borrowers’ 
failure to transition . For longer horizons, classifying all exposure to carbon-intensive sectors as potentially 
stranded assets is overly conservative. A bottom-up approach to transition risk assessment is underdeveloped 
due to the challenges in predicting long-term financials and collection of transition plans.
Transition risk also refers to the need to upgrade the energy effi ciency of real estate objects we finance. It is 
important to note that the translation of EPBD IV into national laws of EU member states is expected in May 
2026. Until then, regulatory uncertainty remains high, which prevents the establishment of a direct link 
between an EPC label  or primary energy demand of real estate objects and a respective level of transition 
risk. For more details, see our transition plans for the commercial and residential real estate sectors. We 
understand that regulatory pressure caused by high environmental impact is already influencing several 
economic sectors (e.g. aviation and automotive). Additional regulation in the future could follow, but its 
impact is not yet known. For the mid-term, we consider transition risk to be significantly covered by our 
Terra approach, which addresses the majority of emissions-intense sectors in ING's Wholesale Banking loan

title: Our transition plan - Introduction
heading: 4.1.5 Our transition plan
start_phrase: At ING, putting sustainability at the heart of what we do is one of the core pillars of our strategy.
summary:
Our transi tion plan
At ING, putting sustainability at the heart of what we do is one of the core pillars of our strategy. Climate 
change is one of the world's biggest challenges, threatening societies as we know them today. We want to 
play our part in the low-carbon transition that’s necessary to achieve a sustainable future. We aim to steer 
the most carbon-intensive parts of our portfolio towards meeting global climate goals and working with 
clients to achieve their own sustainability goals.

society. Our activities are focused on the areas where we believe we can make the greatest impact. For more 
information on our strategy, see ‘Sustainability at the heart ’.

title: Approach to the transition plan
heading: 4.1.5.1 Approach to the transition plan
start_phrase: With the Terra approach, ING measures the emission intensities of clients active in the most carbon-intensive sectors, except for upstream oil & gas which we steer on financial exposures .
summary:
- ING enhanced its climate stress-testing methodology for corporate and mortgage credit risk, building on ICAAP/EBA frameworks with overlays for transition and physical risks.
- It supports clients’ sustainable transition via product offerings and green funding, tracking progress against publicly disclosed commitments (e.g., Terra transition plan, green funding framework) rather than product-level financial effects.
- ING’s Terra transition plan aims to steer carbon‑intensive portfolios toward global climate goals and help clients meet their own sustainability targets.
- Terra approach: measures emission intensities in high‑emitting sectors (upstream oil & gas steered on financial exposure), benchmarks clients to sector decarbonization pathways, measures absolute financed emissions where available, and performs hotspot analyses to manage risks/opportunities.
- Sector transition plans: tailored, GFANZ‑aligned and NZBA‑compliant; currently cover 10 sectors (residential real estate under refinement; aluminium and dairy in development); forthcoming targets, performance, and stakeholder asks outlined in “Our Terra approach.”
- Governance: ING’s management boards approve and oversee the net‑zero commitment, transition planning, and Terra implementation.
- Integration and resources: climate embedded in business planning via Risk Appetite Statements and KPIs to direct lending toward sustainable activities; strong emphasis on data availability, quality, and tooling as critical enablers.
- Decision‑making in Wholesale Banking: mandatory Terra/climate questions in deal approvals; expanded 2024 data‑driven ESG risk assessments consider client alignment to science‑based pathways, CTP ambition, and financial capacity; high‑risk cases escalate to ESR; Climate Risk Appetite and sector metrics set; quarterly/annual climate alignment benchmarks support 2030 targets.
- Client engagement: inclusion‑first approach to help especially carbon‑intensive clients transition; ESG.X tool collects ~2,000 clients’ transition data; clients receive CTP scores (Advanced/Moderate/Low); 2024 use of CTPs to guide strategic engagement with toolkits and training; stricter credit terms or exit for clients unwilling or unable to progress.
text:
Approach  to the transition plan  
With the Terra approach, ING measures the emission intensities of clients active in the most carbon-intensive 
sectors, except for upstream oil & gas which we steer on financial exposures . This information helps us to 
benchmark our clients’ activities against the relevant decarbonisation scenarios per sector. In addition, we 
started collecting information from Client Transition Plan (CTP) assessments in our Wholesale Banking 
portfolio. This increase in data availability will support us in gathering additional insights for the sector-based 
transition plans and enable us to engage more effectively with clients in strategic discussions about their 
transition strategies and identifying opportunities to support them with tailored advice, financing and 
investments solutions. 
By engaging with our clients using this information, we steer our lending portfolio and support them in their 
transition, helping them to drive down the emissions caused by their business activities and financing the 
change that is needed. Additionally, by measuring the absolute financed emissions, where data is available, 
we perform hotspot analyses to monitor the ultimate impact of our lending book, identifying risks and 
opportunities, and defining next steps for expanding the scope of our Terra approach. Contents ING at a glance Strategy, business model
