title: Own workforce strategy – Unlocking our people’s full potential - Introduction
heading: 5.1.3 Own workforce strategy – Unlocking our people’s full potential
start_phrase: ING strives to provide a safe , diverse and inclusive workplace.
summary: Introduces ING’s workforce strategy “Unlocking our people’s full potential,” an enabler of the global “Growing the difference” strategy, aimed at a safe, diverse, and inclusive workplace and supported by global policies, targets, actions, and data-driven insights. The approach considers geopolitics, evolving technology, and changing employee expectations, and is governed through Diversity, Inclusion and Belonging (DIB) structures covering harassment and violence prevention, wellbeing, employment, and disability inclusion to manage material risks (morale, productivity, reputation, operational stability, and legal exposure). Tools such as the Annual Gender Pay Gap Process and the Organizational Health Index inform policy refinement, strategic direction, and regulatory change implementation, complemented by residual risk assessments and ongoing policy reviews. Actions include global accessibility obligations, gender pay gap and equal-pay reporting, work-life balance, and training and skill development, underpinned by the Global Code of Conduct. Accessibility initiatives include the 2022 “Leave no-one Behind” vision and a December 2024 global disability and neuro-inclusion strategy for the workforce.
text:
Own workf orce  strategy  – Unlocking our people’s full potential
ING strives to provide a safe , diverse and inclusive workplace. Unlocking our people’s full potential is the 
strategic approach we take to meet this commitment for our workforce, complemented by our global 
policies, targets, actions and data-driven insights. ‘Growing the difference’, ING’s global strategy, is supported 
by four enablers, including ‘unlocking our people’s full potential’, which encompasses our workforce strategy. 
We consider both external and internal factors, such as geopolitical forces, evolving technology and 
changing employee expectations, as these trends shape our business needs and, consequently, our 
strategy.  For more on ‘unlocking our people’s full potential’, see our ‘ Strategy ’ section.
The governance of our diversity, inclusion and belonging (DIB) strategy, of our measures against harassment 
and violence, and of our initiatives supporting wellbeing, employment, and the inclusion of persons with 
disabilities, is stru ctured in such a way that ING can address its material risks and impacts in a timely and 
effective manner. T hese risks, such as harassment and violence, can result in lower employee morale, 
reduced productivity and harm to ING’s overall reputation and operational instability, as well as potential 
legal claims with financial consequences.  To strengthen our adaptability and resilience, tools like the Annual 
Gender Pay Gap Process and the Organizational Health Index provide valuable insights that guide the 
refinement of our policies, inform strategic direction, and support the implementation of regulatory changes. 
Through ongoing policy reviews, residual risk assessments, and the alignment of processes with evolving 
regulations, we continuously enhance our capacity to manage both current and emerging risks effectively.  
Our approach to diversity, inclusion and belonging is focused on understanding, mutual respect, and 
celebration. We recognise that not everyone experiences work and life in the same way, and so we aim to 
ensure fairness and equity in everything we do. ING has a diversity, inclusion and belonging strategy in place 
to foster an inclusive culture and environment. The strategy focuses  on mitigating potential negative 
impacts and highlights the actions  we take around disability  and gender equality, such as our global 
accessibility obligations, and our reporting on our gender pay gap and equal pay for equal work. These aim 
to ensure fairness for all and mitigate the risk of discrimination. In addition, our employees are expected to 
adhere to our Global Code of Conduct, which complements our strategy and is focused on fostering and 
maintaining a safe working environment. Together with focused initiatives on work-life balance and 
employee training and skill development, the environment we seek to create can enhance employee 
engagement, improve wellbeing, and create a strong and diverse performance culture.
ING introduced its global accessibility strategic vision, ‘Leave no-one Behind’, in 2022, setting out to improve 
the position of our employees and customers with disabilities. This was expanded upon in December 2024 
with the launch of a global strategy for disability and neuro-inclusion for our workforce.Policies, actions and performance

title: Diversity and inclusion policy
heading: 5.1.3.1.1 Diversity and inclusion policy
start_phrase: As a globally operating bank, we are continuously navigating the complexities of global and local regulations.
summary:
- ING’s workforce strategy, “unlocking our people’s full potential,” underpins its global strategy and aims to provide a safe, diverse, and inclusive workplace, informed by external and internal trends.
- Robust governance covers diversity, inclusion and belonging (DIB), anti-harassment and violence, wellbeing, employment, and disability inclusion to manage material risks to morale, productivity, reputation, and legal exposure.
- Data-driven tools (Annual Gender Pay Gap Process, Organizational Health Index) guide policy refinement, strategy, and regulatory alignment; ongoing reviews and residual risk assessments strengthen resilience.
- DIB approach emphasizes fairness, equity, understanding, and celebration of differences, with actions on disability and gender equality (global accessibility obligations, gender pay gap and equal pay reporting), complemented by the Global Code of Conduct, work-life balance initiatives, and skills development.
- Global accessibility vision “Leave no-one Behind” (2022) expanded in December 2024 to a workforce strategy for disability and neuro-inclusion.
- A global D&I policy (aligned with CSRD) sets ambitions and targets, focusing on diversity, gender equality and equal pay, and inclusion of persons with disabilities, with guidance on wellbeing and training.
- The DIB strategy was endorsed by senior management, approved by the Management Board, and supported by the Supervisory Board (Nov 2022); the ESG committee updates the Supervisory Board quarterly.
- Policy commitments include fostering inclusive leadership and belonging, merit-based decisions, annual gender pay and equal pay analyses, D&I training, reasonable accommodations for disabilities, zero discrimination/harassment, and adherence to the Orange Code.
- ING denounces all forms of discrimination; policies align with local laws and, where applicable, stricter international standards (UDHR, ILO, UNGPs, EU directives). Related policies include D&I and Whistleblower, plus human rights and workplace statements.
- Actions, targets, and metrics are informed by external partnerships (e.g., Workplace Pride, Business Disability Forum); ING achieved “Advocate” status in the 2024 Workplace Pride benchmark; continued focus on mitigating risks tied to diversity, inclusion, and pay.
- Leadership and learning: Inclusive Leadership workshops delivered to nearly 250 senior leaders across 13 sessions; DIB Learning Explorer curriculum launched and embedded to reduce discrimination risk.
- Employee voice and allyship: 45+ ERGs (culture, disability, gender, generations, LGBTQI+, race/ethnicity) with Management Board sponsors; structured dialogue and HR engagement inform global and local actions; Inclusion Index in OHI monitors experiences by demographic to enable targeted action.
- Skills and talent development: scalable and curated learning (domain academies, online/in-person, formal/informal) aligned to current/future capability needs; 2024 strategic talent reviews of 5,000+ senior roles to align leadership and skills with business needs.
- Workforce characteristics: disclosures on headcount by gender and country, permanent/temporary hours, no non-guaranteed hours, monthly turnover tracking (9% in 2024, unchanged from 2023), regional full-time/part-time breakdowns; related staff expense and employee numbers referenced in Note 25.
text:
Diversity  and inclusion policy
As a globally operating bank, we are continuously navigating the complexities of global and local 
regulations. In some instances, we set general, globally applicable policies to help address the material risks 
and material negative impacts our workforce may face, with consideration for local laws and regulations 
which may necessitate tailored local policies to ensure full compliance. Our global diversity & inclusion (D&I) 
policy, aligned with and recognised as a policy under the CSRD’s policy definition, outlines our global 
ambitions and targets. Among other things, the D&I policy focuses on the impacts and risks related to 
‘diversity’ and ‘gender equality and equal pay for work of equal value’ and the risks regarding ‘employment 
and inclusion of persons with disabilities’. W e have initiatives and guidance addressing the topics of work-life 
balance (wellbeing) and training and skill development. 
The global D&I policy outlines our approach to creating an inclusive culture and environment where 
everyone can be themselves and reach their full potential. Our global diversity, inclusion and belonging 
strategy was endorsed  by ING’s senior management, approved by the Management Boar d and supported by 
the Supervisory Board in November 2022 to work towards the ambitions set out in our global D&I policy. The 
Supervisory Board is informed by th e ESG committee  on related developments on a quarterly basis. O ur D&I 
policy drives us t o:
•actively support diversity, equity, and inclusion, and embed a culture where everyone is valued and 
treated with dignity and respect;•ensure that people leaders work in partnership with their teams to create and sustain an inclusive 
working environment where everyone’s unique contribution is valued and where everyone feels a sense 
of belonging;•ensure that decisions affecting employment, learning and development, promotion and career 
development are based on an individual's ability and reflect genuine requirements of the job;•conduct annual analyses of our global gender pay gap and equal pay for equal work as part of our 
commitment to denounce discrimination and to promote equal remuneration for work of equal value for 
all employees; •provide everyone with the appropriate information, and training, on diversity, equity, and inclusion in the 
workplace;•make the necessary adjustments to meet the needs of people with disabilities where reasonable and 
practicable to do so;
•strive continually to provide people with a working environment that is free from discrimination and/or 
harassment of any kind; and•behave in accordance with the values and behaviours of our Orange Code, which applies to all ING 
business units in all countries worldwide.  Contents ING at a glance Strategy, business model

ING Group Annual  Report 2024  137 At ING, we denounce all forms of discrimination. Our global D&I policy and global DIB strategy, gender 
diversity targets, and various  DIB action plans are aimed at preventing discrimination and driving inclusion. 
Discrimination includes any distinction, exclusion or preference made on the basis of age, sex, gender 
identity or expression, gender reassignment, sexual orientation, family responsibility (including pregnancy, 
maternity, paternity and adoption), partnership status, cultural background, religion, race, ethnicity, physical 
or mental disability, nationality, political opinion, social origin or any other status, that has the effect of 
nullifying or impairing equal opportunity or treatment in employment. Any distinction, exclusion or 
preference not based on the inherent requirements of the job is deemed as discrimination. 
ING’s workforce policies are aligned with local labour laws and regulations in all countries where we have 
operations. In countries where local legislation goes further than the principles set out by the Universal 
Declaration of Human Rights and ILO Core Conventions, we also apply additional and stricter requirements. 
In addition, we seek alignment with international standards on human rights (such as the UNGPs) through 
the implementation of EU d irectives  and the development of internal policies, such as our D&I policy, 
Whistleblower policy and other mechanisms, such as our human rights statement and workplace statement . 
Our D&I policy is available on ing.com.

title: Actions, targets and metrics
heading: 5.1.3.1.2 Actions, targets and metrics
start_phrase: We take various actions to further understand the impacts coming from outside ING, and we continuously inform our workforce and leaders on best practices related to developments and learnings in DIB.
summary:
- Strong anti-discrimination stance backed by a global Diversity & Inclusion (D&I) policy and Diversity, Inclusion and Belonging (DIB) strategy, including gender diversity targets and action plans; clear definition of discrimination and commitment that any non–job-related distinction is prohibited.
- Compliance with local labor laws across all operations and alignment with international human rights standards (Universal Declaration of Human Rights, ILO Core Conventions, UNGPs), EU directives, and internal policies (D&I policy, Whistleblower policy, human rights and workplace statements).
- Actions, targets, and metrics to understand and respond to external impacts on DIB, including partnerships with Workplace Pride and the Business Disability Forum; participation in external assessments; recognition as an “Advocate” in the 2024 Workplace Pride global benchmark; focus on mitigating risks around inclusion, gender pay, and remuneration.
- Leadership and learning initiatives: rollout of Inclusive Leadership workshops to nearly 250 senior leaders across MBB, leadership teams, and country Executive Committees; launch and promotion of the DIB Learning Explorer curriculum to deepen understanding, self-awareness, and reduce discriminatory behavior.
- Employee engagement and feedback mechanisms: 45+ global Employee Resource Groups (ERGs) across multiple identity areas with Management Board sponsors; structured dialogue with ERG leaders and country HR teams to surface and address inclusion challenges; annual Inclusion Index in the OHI survey to track inclusion by gender, age, and organizational demographics and enable targeted actions.
- Talent and skills development: scalable and curated learning offerings (domain academies, mandatory/non-mandatory, online/in-person, formal/informal) to meet current and future capability needs; 2024 strategic talent reviews for 5,000+ senior roles to align leadership, skills, and capabilities with business needs.
- Workforce characteristics and disclosures: headcount breakdowns by gender and country for significant locations; details on permanent and temporary hours; no non‑guaranteed working hours (on-call employees have fixed hours); monthly turnover tracking with total turnover at 9% in 2024 (unchanged from 2023); full-time/part-time breakdowns by region; related staff expenses and employee numbers disclosed in Note 25 “Staff expenses.”
text:
We take various actions to further understand the impacts coming from outside ING, and we continuously 
inform our workforce and leaders on best practices related to developments and learnings in DIB. This is 
exemplified in our collaboration with external organisations to understand the impact of global events, 
socio-economic movements, and changes in legislation on DIB. For example, we make the most of our 
memberships of Workplace Pride and the Business Disability Forum to draw on their expertise and guidance 
to refine our strategy and actions for, respectively, the LGBTQI+ and disability communities. Where 
appropriate, we participate in external assessments, to understand our maturity on specific areas and our 
need for focus and improvement in others. In 2024 , ING was named as an ‘Advocate’ in the annual 
Workplace Pride global benchmark , the highest ranking possible for an organisation . ING continues to 
investigate how we can further mitigate potential negative impacts and risks on our own workforce within 
the scope of diversity, inclusion and belonging, gender pay and remuneration.
During the course of 2023 and 2024, we rolled out the ‘Inclusive Leadership’ workshop across the MBB , their 
leadership teams and country Executive Committees. Across 13 workshops attended by a total of nearly 250 
leaders, participants gained an understanding of how the global DIB strategy supports the bank’s strategy 
and were empowered to take practical action to create a more inclusive ING and more connected teams. We 
also developed and launched the DIB Learning Explorer curriculum in 2023 and are continuing to promote 
and embed this across the business. By fostering self-awareness among our workforce and leaders and 
deepening the understanding of diversity and inclusion, we help to reduce the risk of discriminatory 
behaviour within the organisation.Our efforts go beyond formal training and skill development, actively promoting inclusion, self-awareness 
and allyship through our employee resource groups (ERGs) and continuous listening. There are over 45 ERGs 
globally relating to culture, disability, gender, generations, LGBTQI+, and race and ethnicity, with members of 
our Management Board as sponsors. Through structured dialogue with the leaders of our ERGs across ING, 
the global DIB team can gather feedback on people's experiences. This is used to help shape ING’s global DIB 
strategy and associated actions, both at a global and local level. Similarly, ongoing engagement with 
country HR teams creates additional channels for any inclusion-related challenges to be raised. Efforts are 
made to resolve issues collaboratively and as far as is possible. In addition, we have incorporated a yearly 
Inclusion Index in our OHI survey to analyse different experiences of inclusion based on gender, age, and 
organisational demographic, enabling us to monitor the effectiveness of the policy  and allowing us to take 
targeted action where required.

title: Actions on training and skill development
heading: 5.1.3.1.3 Actions on training and skill development
start_phrase: Through our engagement with our workforce, we understand that to drive meaningful change, we must attract, develop, and retain fit-for-future talents.
summary:
- States a zero-tolerance stance on discrimination and defines it comprehensively across protected characteristics; outlines a global D&I policy and DIB strategy with gender diversity targets and action plans to prevent discrimination and foster inclusion.
- Confirms alignment with local labor laws across all countries and, where relevant, application of stricter standards than UDHR/ILO principles; seeks alignment with international human rights standards (UNGPs), EU directives, and internal policies (D&I, Whistleblower, human rights and workplace statements).
- Describes actions, targets, and metrics: collaboration with Workplace Pride and the Business Disability Forum to refine approaches for LGBTQI+ and disability inclusion; participation in external assessments; recognition as an “Advocate” in the 2024 Workplace Pride global benchmark; ongoing work to mitigate risks related to diversity, inclusion, belonging, and gender pay/remuneration.
- Details leadership enablement: 13 Inclusive Leadership workshops in 2023–2024 for MBB, leadership teams, and country Executive Committees (nearly 250 leaders), tying DIB to business strategy and practical actions; launch and adoption of the DIB Learning Explorer curriculum.
- Highlights culture and engagement mechanisms: 45+ global employee resource groups (ERGs) across multiple dimensions with Management Board sponsors; structured dialogue and continuous listening to inform global and local DIB actions; engagement with country HR teams to surface and address inclusion challenges; annual Inclusion Index in the OHI survey to monitor inclusion by demographics and guide targeted actions.
- Covers training and talent development: scalable, curated L&D offerings (domain academies; mandatory/non-mandatory, online/in-person; formal/informal); 2024 strategic talent reviews for 5,000+ senior roles to align leadership, skills, and capability needs.
- Provides workforce characteristics and disclosures: headcount with gender and country breakdowns for significant locations; permanent vs temporary hours; no non-guaranteed working hours (on-call agreements have fixed hours); monthly turnover measurement with 2024 turnover at 9% (unchanged from 2023); regional breakdowns of full-time and part-time employees; references to staff expenses and employee numbers in the consolidated financial statements (Note 25).
text:
Actions on training and skill development
Through our engagement with our workforce, we understand that to drive meaningful change, we must 
attract, develop, and retain fit-for-future talents. Therefore, we have both scalable and curated learning and 
development offerings tailored to our employees’ roles and growth to meet our current and future skills and 
capability needs. This includes domain-level academies, mandatory and non-mandatory learnings (online 
and in-person) and both formal and informal development opportunities for our range of employee scales. 
To complement our training agenda we also focus on talent development. In 2024 we performed strategic 
talent reviews across the bank for more than 5,000 senior roles in order to better identify and understand 
the leadership, skill and capability needs of our domains to grow the difference.

title: Actions and targets on gender diversity
heading: 5.1.3.1.5 Actions and targets on gender diversity
start_phrase: In order to more systemically address the representation of women in senior leadership, a bank-wide gender equity action plan was launched in 2022.
summary:
- A bank-wide gender equity action plan (launched in 2022) targets sustainable improvements in hiring, progression, and retention of women, informed by gender pay gap (GPG) and equal pay for equal work analyses to address pay and performance inequities.
- Governance links: gender-related targets for women in leadership are set with approval from the Management Board Banking (MBB) and Supervisory Board; part of Executive Board and MBB variable pay is tied to delivering these targets.
- Target-setting process: the Global Head of Diversity, Inclusion & Belonging proposes annual targets to HR, then to MBB and the Supervisory Board for approval; worker representatives are not involved. Commitments are public; progress is tracked internally and shared with HR leaders and senior business leaders, and reported quarterly to the MBB and the Supervisory Board ESG committee.
- Broader inclusion measures include increasing women in leadership and introducing global guidelines in 2025 for equitable parental leave transitions, ensuring consistent support and equal access to career development before, during, and after leave.
- Pay equity framework: “Our People Offer” and the ING Remuneration Regulation Framework require gender-neutral fixed/variable pay and benefits; ongoing analyses aim to remove structural barriers to gender equity.
- GPG methodology: ING has measured the GPG since 2021; a 2022 baseline was established. The 2024 analysis includes fixed pay and variable remuneration and, due to new regulations, reports for the current year using target variable remuneration (rather than actuals used in 2022–2023). Both unadjusted and adjusted GPG are assessed.
- Equal pay for equal work: assessments use the Global Job Architecture to compare roles of equal value across locations and lines; results were shared with senior leaders and highlight areas requiring attention.
- Leadership diversity framework: diverse leadership is positioned as improving decision-making. Under the Netherlands Gender Diversity Act (2022), the Executive Board target is 30% women, and the Supervisory Board quota is at least one-third women and one-third men.
- Bank-wide gender targets: at least 35% women in senior leadership by 2028, and at least 30% women in the leadership pipeline by 2025.
text:
In order to more systemically address the representation of women in senior leadership, a bank-wide gender 
equity action plan was launched in 2022. This was aimed at making sustainable improvements to how we 
hire, progress, and retain female talent. This action plan includes results from our gender pay gap and equal 
pay for equal work analyses, which are designed to highlight disparity and seek to address the inequities 
that exist in relation to pay and performance. There is also a set of gender-related targets focused on the 
representation of women in leadership roles as agreed by the Management  Board Banking (MBB). A part of 
the variable pay  of our Executive Board and Management Board Banking is linked to the delivery of these 
internal targets on gender diversity.
The global head  of Diversity, Inclusion & Belonging proposes annual gender diversity targets to the HR 
Management Team, after which they are discussed with the MBB and Supervisory Board for final approval. The 
workforce or workers’ representatives  are not involved in this process , but these commitments are shared 
externally  and are publicly available. We track progress against these gender diversity targets internally, and 
the results are shared with global domain HR directors and relevant senior business leaders to drive progress . 
This progress is also shared quarterly with both the MBB and Supervisory Board ESG committee.  One of our efforts to boost broader diverse representation is by striving to increase the number of women in 
leadership roles. See ‘ Unlocking our people’s full potential ’ to learn about progress on our efforts. In addition 
to these gender targets, we are enhancing our gender equity awareness and broadening our scope with the 
launch of new global guidelines and standards for successful parental leave transitions in 2025, designed to 
enhance the support previously in place for people leaving and returning to the bank when having a family. 
These global guidelines aim to ensure equal support for all working parents, before, during and after parental 
leave with a focus on equal access to career development opportunities.

title: Actions regarding gender pay gap (GPG) and ‘equal pay for equal work’ metrics - Introduction
heading: 5.1.3.1.6 Actions regarding gender pay gap (GPG) and ‘equal pay for equal work’ metrics
start_phrase: At ING we have defined ‘ Our people offer’ (OPO) which describes how we want to pay and treat our employees fairly and transparently .
summary: Introduces ING’s framework for fair, gender‑neutral pay under its Our People Offer and ING Remuneration Regulation Framework, explaining how the bank measures the gender pay gap (GPG) and equal pay for equal work. ING uses an externally assessed, two-part GPG methodology (unadjusted and adjusted) and, in 2024, revised calculations to meet new regulatory requirements by reporting for the current year using fixed pay plus target variable remuneration (instead of prior years’ actual VR); VR schemes are gender‑neutral, based on the Global Job Architecture (GJA), and expressed as a percentage of fixed pay. Equal pay analyses leverage the GJA to compare roles across countries and business lines; findings are shared with senior leaders, justified pay differences are affirmed, and unjustified gaps are corrected. The section also notes groundwork laid in 2022 to baseline gaps from 2021 and outlines Dutch Gender Diversity Act expectations (Executive Board target 30%; Supervisory Board quota one‑third women and one‑third men) alongside ING’s bank‑wide goals of at least 35% women in senior leadership by 2028 and 30% women in the leadership pipeline by 2025.
text:
Actions regarding gender pay gap (GPG) and ‘equal pay for equal work’ metrics 
At ING we have defined ‘ Our people offer’ (OPO) which describes  how we want to pay and treat our 
employees  fairly and transparently . We ensure that all our remuneration schemes (fixed and variable) and 
our benefit  schemes are gender neutral, which is also stated in our ING Remuneration Regulation Framework 
(IRRF). Through OPO and our commitment to fair and transparent pay, we actively analyse reward practices 
to understand and remove structural barriers in the drive towards gender equity. 
The gender pay gap (i.e. the difference between the average remuneration of men and women) is one of the 
measurements we use towards this commitment and is a practice ING committed itself to in 2021 ahead of 
industry standards and regulatory requirements. In 2022, we laid the groundwork to understand gender pay 
more thoroughly, and to provide a baseline to understand any gaps from 2021 onwards. Our analysis, 
supported by an externally assessed methodology, is divided into two parts: unadjusted gender pay gap and 
adjusted gender pay gap. This two-fold approach allows for more nuance, which is necessary given the 
complexity of the topic and change in analysis compared to previous years: 
•The 2024 gender pay gap calculation methodology continues to use fixed compensation and variable 
remuneration (VR)1, but has been adjusted following new regulatory requirements mandating reporting 
of the GPG for the respective reporting year. Previously, ING reflected the GPG with a one-year gap. •To accommodate reporting for the current fiscal year, the 2024 GPG analysis used a target variable 
remuneration figure instead of the actual paid variable remuneration, the latter of which was used for the 
2022 and  2023 analyses. This VR target2 represents the expected bonus an employee may receive based 
on the target performance of the Group, business line or functions and the individual.
Separate to the gender pay gap, we also initiated equal pay for equal work analyses to assess whether there 
is equal remuneration for men and women for work done of equal value. We use our Global Job Architecture 
(GJA) to aid this analysis, which organises all job profiles within ING into a standardised structure allowing for 
easier comparison of capabilities and accountabilities across countries and business lines. Using this 
architecture, we were able to perform an ‘equal pay for equal work’ assessment and the results were shared

title: Unadjusted gender pay gap
heading: 5.1.3.1.6.1 Unadjusted gender pay gap
start_phrase: ING follows the guidelines laid out by the European Banking Authority (EBA), which collects benchmarking data on the gender pay gap from banks under its supervision (including ING) per fiscal year as of 2023.
summary:
- Describes ING’s approach to pay equity: justified pay differences are reviewed and affirmed; unjustified differences trigger corrective action to ensure parity.
- Explains compliance with European Banking Authority (EBA) gender pay gap benchmarking and ING’s early global reporting of both unadjusted and adjusted gaps.
- Defines the unadjusted gender pay gap (UGPG) per EBA as the difference in mean remuneration between men and women as a percentage of men’s mean remuneration.
- Reports ING’s global UGPG: 28% in 2024 (down from 31% in 2023 and 32% in 2022). Attributes the gap mainly to higher male representation in senior, higher‑paid roles and to career events (new joiners/leavers and internal mobility; level and compensation changes).
- Notes a 2024 methodology change using annual fixed pay plus target bonus (instead of actual paid bonus); ING will assess its impact and publish the 2024 UGPG with actual bonuses in the 2025 Annual Report.
- Presents adjusted gender pay gap (AGPG) analysis using the Oaxaca‑Blinder method, controlling chiefly for country differences and job classification (Global Job Architecture). Method includes “centralising” hourly rates by country averages to isolate structural differences.
- Indicates drivers of the adjusted analysis: 1.11% explained by country differences and 2.15% by job profile distribution, with higher male proportionality in certain better‑paid profiles contributing to the gap.
- States global AGPG results: 2% in 2024 and 2023 (3% in 2022), implying women earn on average 98% of men’s pay after adjustments; underscores commitment to increasing women’s representation in senior roles.
- Provides a country/entity table (headcount >250) with UGPG and AGPG for 2022–2024, showing generally sizable unadjusted gaps alongside small adjusted gaps (often 0–3%), with some entities showing near‑zero or negative adjusted gaps.
text:
Unadjusted gender pay gap  
ING follows the guidelines laid out by the European Banking Authority (EBA), which collects benchmarking 
data on the gender pay gap from banks under its supervision (including ING) per fiscal year as of 2023. ING is 
ahead of this requirement, having begun collecting data on gender pay globally and publishing its 
unadjusted and adjusted global gender pay gap in 2022. Using the EBA’s definition, the unadjusted gender 
pay gap represents the difference in the mean remuneration paid to men and women expressed as a 
percentage of the mean remuneration paid to men. 
 
For 2024, using annual fixed remuneration and target bonus, the unadjusted gender pay gap of ING globally 
was 28 percent . Comparatively, a t the end of 2023, the unadjusted gender pay gap of ING globally was 31 
percent , and at year-end 2022  it was 32 percent .
According to our analysis, this gap is caused by the higher representation of men in more senior, higher-
paying roles than women . The difference between the unadjusted gender pay gap of ING globally can be 
mainly explained by career events, such as i) new joiners and leavers (including internal mobility), ii) 
compensation changes together with level changes, and iii) compensation changes without other changes.  
In the course of 2025, we will analyse whether the change in methodology, from actual paid bonus to target 
bonus, had a (significant) impact on the results. In the Annual Report 2025, we will also publish the 2024 
unadjusted gender pay gap using the actual paid bonuses .
The results of ING’s global unadjusted gender pay gap reinforce  our aim to increase the representation of 
women in senior roles. To strengthen our understanding of the unadjusted gender pay gap, we conducted a 
deeper analysis to assess where and why these differences in pay between men and women occur. This next 
level of work is known as our ‘

title: Adjusted gender pay gap
heading: 5.1.3.1.6.2 Adjusted gender pay gap
start_phrase: Our adjusted gender pay gap analysis accounts for several factors to make the comparisons meaningful, including two main drivers: country differences and job classification.
summary:
- Focus: ING’s reporting on gender pay gaps, distinguishing between unadjusted and adjusted measures, methodology, results for 2024 with comparisons to 2023 and 2022, drivers of differences, and actions to improve parity.

- Governance and scope:
  - Aligned with European Banking Authority (EBA) guidelines; ING has been publishing global unadjusted and adjusted gender pay gaps since 2022, ahead of formal requirements.
  - Commitment to review pay differences, affirm justified cases, and correct unjustified disparities.

- Unadjusted gender pay gap (UGPG):
  - Definition: Difference in mean remuneration between men and women, expressed as a percentage of men’s mean pay (2024 based on annual fixed pay plus target bonus).
  - Global results: 28% in 2024 (down from 31% in 2023 and 32% in 2022).
  - Key drivers: Higher male representation in senior, higher‑paying roles; career events (new joiners/leavers, internal mobility); compensation changes with/without level changes.
  - Methodology note: Shift from actual paid bonus to target bonus in 2024; ING will assess impact and also publish 2024 figures using actual paid bonuses in the 2025 Annual Report.

- Adjusted gender pay gap (AGPG):
  - Method: Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition controlling for meaningful factors.
  - Main explanatory factors:
    - Country differences (1.11% effect): Addressed by centralizing hourly rates to country averages.
    - Job classification via Global Job Architecture (2.15% effect): Certain job profiles with higher pay have higher male representation.
  - Results: 2% globally in 2024 (2% in 2023; 3% in 2022), indicating women are paid on average 98% of men when adjusting for these factors.
  - Ongoing priority: Reduce under‑representation of women in leadership roles.

- Country/entity breakdown (headcount >250):
  - Detailed table provides UGPG and AGPG for 2022–2024 across major ING entities.
  - Typical pattern: UGPGs range roughly 8%–32% across countries; AGPGs generally cluster around 0%–3%, with a few near-zero or slightly negative results.
  - Illustrative highlights (2024):
    - ING Group: UGPG 28%, AGPG 2%.
    - Netherlands: UGPG 16%, AGPG 1%.
    - United Kingdom: UGPG 32%, AGPG 2%.
    - Poland (Slaski): UGPG 31%, AGPG 3%.
    - Germany: UGPG 15%, AGPG 1%.
    - Spain: UGPG 14%, AGPG 2%.
    - Italy: UGPG 17%, AGPG −1%.
    - Singapore: UGPG 31%, AGPG −1%.
    - Philippines Hub: UGPG 27%, AGPG 0%.
    - United States: UGPG 24%, AGPG 1%.
  - Trend: Modest year‑over‑year improvements in UGPG in several markets; AGPGs largely stable and low.
text:
Adjusted gender pay gap 
Our adjusted gender pay gap analysis accounts for several factors to make the comparisons meaningful, 
including two main drivers: country differences and job classification. ING calculates its adjusted gender pay 
following the Oaxaca-Blinder method. 
The adjusted gender gap analysis shows a 2 percent  globa l pay gap for 2024 ( 2 percent  for 2023):
1.11 percent is explained by country differences, i.e. there are structural pay differences between countries. 
To reduce the variance between countries, we ‘centralise’ each employee’s hourly rate by taking the 
country average hourly rate as the ‘centre’. From this, a new average can be calculated for each gender. 
Separating the impact of these structural differences allows a fairer comparison;2.15 percent is explained predominantly by ING’s job framework, Global Job Architecture (GJA). Working in 
certain job profiles has a positive effect on salary (compared to the majority role taken as reference). In 
these job profiles there are more male than female employees. In conclusion, the higher proportionality 
of men partially drives the gap.  
By subtracting the effects of country differences and our GJA , the adjusted gender pay gap was 2 percent  in 
2024 and 2 percent  at year-end 2023 (2022: 3 percent ). Therefore, we found that female employees are paid 
on average 98 percent in 2024  (2023: 98 percent) of what male employees are paid. While we are 
encouraged by the fact that our adjusted gender pay gap shows there are objective, explainable reasons for 
our unadjusted pay gap, we realise there is more to be done, especially about the under-representation of 
women in leadership positions, and we remain fully committed to improving this.

title: Remuneration ratio
heading: 5.1.3.1.7 Remuneration ratio
start_phrase: In line with the ESRS definition, the total remuneration ratio for 2024 is 1:32 , meaning the highest paid employee receives 32 times the median remuneration.
summary:
- Remuneration ratios: ING reports a 2024 ESRS total remuneration ratio of 1:32 (highest-paid employee to median), calculated using annualised fixed and variable pay based on the VR target and including base salary, role-based and collective allowances, discretionary and collective variable remuneration, sales incentives, incidental VR, retention awards, and annual variable allowances. Under the Dutch Corporate Governance Code, the CEO internal ratio for 2024 is 1:24; further details are in the Remuneration report.
- Work-life balance initiatives: ING promotes flexible working through hybrid and international remote work and a range of paid time-off options (e.g., parental, diversity, and care leave) tailored to local laws. In 2024, it launched “Working habits,” a tech-enabled program with global manager training to foster healthy, effective work practices, and is developing a global wellbeing strategy for 2025.
- Disability and neurodiversity actions: ING’s Global Accessibility & Inclusivity Centre of Excellence drives universal design across digital and physical environments. Mandatory accessibility obligations are being embedded in internal policies to set a global standard, and accessibility is integrated into the ESG risk framework. In 2024, ING introduced a global disability and neuro-inclusion strategy with required actions for all countries during 2025–2027, alongside ongoing awareness campaigns (e.g., GAAD, IDPD) to build an open, safe, and caring culture.
- Whistleblower policy and workplace conduct: ING’s Whistleblower Policy guides careful, lawful handling of human-rights-related concerns. The company reinforces its Orange Code and Global Code of Conduct and provides confidential channels (e.g., OHI survey, whistleblower process), training, and intranet resources. Concerns are tracked and reported quarterly up to the Supervisory Board Risk Committee, categorized under discrimination; aggression/violence/bullying; breach of employee confidentiality/data privacy; (sexual) harassment; work pressure/unrealistic targets; and retaliation.
text:
Remuneration  ratio 
In line with the ESRS definition, the total remuneration ratio for 2024 is 1:32 , meaning the highest paid 
employee receives 32 times the median remuneration.  We determined the ratio of the total remuneration 
(i.e. the annualised total fixed and variable remuneration (VR) based on the VR target) of the highest paid 
employee in ING compared to the median total remuneration of all ING staff, excluding the highest paid 
employee. Total remuneration includes base salary, role-based allowance, fixed collective allowances, 
discretionary VR, collective VR, sales incentive, other incidental VR, retention award, and annual variable 
allowances .
ING is also required to disclose the internal ratio based on the Dutch Corporate Governance Code , which 
deviates from the remuneration ratio mentioned above, as it concerns "the ratio between (i) the total annual 
remuneration of the CEO and (ii) the average annual remuneration of the employees of ING". The internal 
ratio for the CEO in 2024 was 1:24. For more information, see our ‘ Remuneration report ’.

title: Actions on work-life balance
heading: 5.1.3.1.8 Actions on work-life balance
start_phrase: At ING we consider a healthy work-life balance important for sustainable and engaged employees.
summary:
- Remuneration ratios: ING reports a 2024 ESRS-defined total remuneration ratio of 1:32 (highest-paid employee to median employee), detailing included pay elements (base salary, role-based and collective allowances, discretionary and collective variable remuneration, sales incentives, incidental VR, retention awards, annual variable allowances). The Dutch Corporate Governance Code internal ratio (CEO to average employee) is 1:24.  
- Work-life balance: Emphasis on flexible working (hybrid and international remote), country-specific paid leave (e.g., parental, diversity, care leave), and the 2024 launch of “Working habits,” a tech-enabled program with manager training to embed healthy, effective ways of working. ING is developing a global wellbeing strategy for 2025 covering mental and physical health and work-life balance.  
- Disability and neurodiversity: A Global Accessibility & Inclusivity Centre of Excellence drives universal design across digital and physical environments. ING is embedding mandatory accessibility obligations into internal policies to create a global standard, with accessibility integrated in the ESG risk framework. A new global disability and neuro-inclusion strategy (2025–2027) sets actions for all countries; ongoing awareness efforts include GAAD and IDPD to foster an open, safe, caring culture and encourage sharing lived experiences.  
- Whistleblower and anti-harassment measures: The Whistleblower Policy guides careful, lawful, timely handling of human rights-related concerns. text:
Actions on work-life balance
At ING we consider a healthy work-life balance important for sustainable and engaged employees. We 
promote a flexible way of working among our employees through different programmes such as hybrid 
working, international remote working, and various paid-time off programmes in order to support our 
employees in distinct phases of their lives. Our broad range of family-related or personal event-related leave, 
such as parental leave, diversity leave and care leave, is country-dependent and in compliance with local 
legislation and requirements. 
In 2024, we launched ING’s ‘Working habits’, which provides tailored insights and proposals for healthy and 
effective ways of working. This scalable technology is enhanced by global training for our managers which 
equips them with practical tips to adopt ‘best practice’ working habits with their teams. As part of our 
ambition to promote wellbeing, including mental wellbeing, physical wellbeing, and a healthy work-life 
balance, we are working towards a global wellbeing strategy in 2025.

title: Actions on disability and neurodiversity
heading: 5.1.3.1.9 Actions on disability and neurodiversity
start_phrase: We recognise our role in supporting disability inclusion and our responsibility to provide accessibility in banking and employment, in support of our employees and customers with and without disabilities.
summary:
- Remuneration ratios: ING reports a 2024 ESRS-defined total remuneration ratio of 1:32 (highest-paid employee to median employee), calculated on annualized fixed and target variable pay and including all relevant allowances and incentives. Under the Dutch Corporate Governance Code, the internal CEO-to-average employee ratio is 1:24. Further details are in the Remuneration report.
- Work-life balance: ING promotes flexible work through hybrid and international remote working and country-specific paid leave (parental, diversity, care). In 2024 it launched “Working habits,” a tool with tailored insights and manager training to improve healthy, effective work practices, and is developing a global wellbeing strategy for 2025 covering mental and physical wellbeing and work-life balance.
- Disability and neurodiversity: A Global Accessibility & Inclusivity Centre of Excellence drives universal design across digital and physical environments. ING is embedding mandatory accessibility obligations into policies, setting a global internal accessibility standard, and integrating accessibility into its ESG risk framework. A new global disability and neuro-inclusion strategy launched in 2024 includes country-level actions for 2025–2027 and ongoing awareness campaigns (e.g., GAAD, IDPD) to foster an open, safe, and supportive culture.
- Whistleblower and anti-violence/harassment measures: The Whistleblower Policy guides careful, lawful handling of human rights-related concerns, including violence and harassment. Employees are encouraged to speak up via confidential channels (OHI survey, whistleblower process) supported by guidance and training. Concerns are recorded, monitored, and reported quarterly up to the Supervisory Board Risk Committee, categorized as discrimination; aggression/violence/bullying; employee-related confidentiality/data privacy breaches; (sexual) harassment; work pressure/unrealistic targets; and retaliation.
text:
Actions on disability and neurodiversity   
We recognise our role in supporting disability inclusion and our responsibility to provide accessibility in 
banking and employment, in support of our employees and customers with and without disabilities. ING has 
an existing Global Accessibility & Inclusivity Centre of Excellence (CoE) that is responsible for ensuring our 
digital and physical environment is accessible for all at ING through universal design. ING is currently 
implementing mandatory accessibility obligations throughout its internal policies with the aim of informing 
ING employees of their responsibilities more thoroughly in delivering an accessible bank for persons with 
disabilities and/or neurodiversity. With these accessibility obligations, we aim to set an internal global 
standard for accessibility. Accessibility is also a part of the ING ESG risk framework. 
In 2024, ING introduced a new global disability and neuro-inclusion strategy, aimed at breaking down the 
barriers people face and ensuring everyone has the support they need to thrive. During a three-year period between 2025 and 2027, all countries across ING will be expected to take several strategic actions to help 
drive change, create more equity and improve people’s experience at ING no matter where they work and 
what they do. Furthermore, we will continue to share our accessibility efforts through global internal and 
external communications on disability awareness-related days, including Global Accessibility Awareness Day 
(GAAD) and International Day for Persons with Disabilities (IDPD). The purpose is to raise awareness of key 
topics and build understanding within the organisation, contributing to an open, safe, and caring culture and 
to encourage people to share their lived experiences so we can better support them.

title: Our actions against violence and harassment in the workplace
heading: 5.1.3.1.11 Our actions against violence and harassment in the workplace
start_phrase: We are committed to upholding both the requirements set by human rights, laws, and regulations, as well as the exacting standards of our Orange Code and Global Code of Conduct, through which we can fulfil our purpose of empowering people while countering potential negative impacts and risks related to, for example, violence and harassment.
summary:

text:
Our actions against  violence and harassment in the workplace
We are committed to upholding both the requirements set by human rights, laws, and regulations, as well 
as the exacting standards of our Orange Code and Global Code of Conduct, through which we can fulfil our 
purpose of empowering people while countering potential negative impacts and risks related to, for example, 
violence and harassment. We encourage employees to share concerns in confidentiality and speak up 
through multiple initiatives and channels, such as the OHI survey and the w histleblower process . These 
channels are globally known, encompass mature processes  and are made available on ING’s intranet, with 
guidance and trainings additionally available so employees and managers have a full understanding of the 
infrastructure in place. Read more about our Global Code of Conduct in the Governance  section.

title: Consumers and end-users - Introduction
heading: 5.2 Consumers and end-users
start_phrase: Consumers an d end-users of ING’s services include companies and private individuals who we provide our services to.
summary: Introduction to ING’s “Consumers and end-users” focus: defines consumers as companies and private individuals but, based on a double materiality assessment, concentrates on private individual customers in Retail Banking. States commitments to fair product access, transparent communication, and respecting customer rights, with risk mitigation around access to quality information, social inclusion, and privacy. Highlights particular relevance to customers in vulnerable positions, defining vulnerability and citing examples (elderly; those with temporary sensory, physical, cognitive, neurodiverse disabilities; chronic disease; reading difficulties). Signals forthcoming identification of impacts, risks, and opportunities.
text:
Consumers  and end-users
Consumers an d end-users of ING’s services include companies  and private individuals who we provide our 
services to. In accordance with the outcome of the double materiality assessment,  we focus this section on 
private individual customers within our Retail Banking domain , also referred to as our ‘customers’. At ING, we 
strive to make access to our products fair and our communication transparent, and to respect the rights of 
our customers when providing our services. This includes mitigating impacts and risks related to access to 
quality information, social inclusion, and privacy.  
We assessed the materiality  in acknowledgement that the topics are particularly relevant to customers in a 
vulnerable position . A customer is in a vulnerable position when, due to their personal circumstances, they 
are especially susceptible to harm or exclusion , particularly when ING is not acting with appropriate levels of 
care. Customers in a vulnerable position may include e lderly customers, customers who experience 
(temporary) sensory, physical, cognitive, neurodiverse disabilities, or chronic disease and customers with 
reading difficulties.

title: Identified impacts, risks and opportunities
heading: 5.2.1 Identified impacts, risks and opportunities
start_phrase: Negative impacts relate to practices that compromise fairness, inclusivity, and data security and can harm customer wellbeing, damage our reputation, and expose us to financial and regulatory risks.
summary:
- Scope and focus: Centers on private individual customers in ING’s Retail Banking, following a double materiality assessment. Emphasizes fair access, transparent communication, and respect for customer rights, with attention to access to quality information, social inclusion, and privacy.
- Vulnerable customers: Defines vulnerability as heightened susceptibility to harm or exclusion due to personal circumstances. Examples include elderly people, individuals with temporary or permanent sensory, physical, cognitive, neurodiverse disabilities or chronic disease, and customers with reading difficulties.
- Identified negative impacts and risks:
  - Access to quality information: Risks of unfair customer treatment through mis-selling, misrepresentation, or unclear product presentations, potentially causing financial distress.
  - Social inclusion: Potential non-discrimination violations, lack of access due to accessibility barriers or regional restrictions, unequal treatment, and misleading marketing.
  - Privacy: Data protection failures (e.g., GDPR breaches) could lead to identity theft, financial loss, loss of privacy, and emotional distress.
  - Associated risks include reputational, financial, and regulatory exposure if fairness, inclusivity, and data security are not upheld.
- Financial effects: Assessed through customer engagement, complaints channels, and legal claims, using the provisions and legal proceedings framework in the financial statements. No significant financial effects reported for 2024.
- Customer engagement and governance: Engagement led by the head of Retail. Tools include annual Net Promoter Score (NPS), complaints channels, and inclusive design practices supported by the Global Centre of Expertise (CoE) Accessibility.
- External accessibility engagement: CoE Accessibility participates in global accessibility forums (e.g., Zero Project, European Platform for Rehabilitation, Social Services Europe), using insights to refine actions across ING. Outcomes include the EAA Compliance Program and a joint report with Sia-Partners (Jan 2024) on the European Accessibility Act’s impact on banking services.
- Customer strategy—Superior customer value: Aims to make banking easy, instant, personal, and relevant; ensure clear pricing and plain language; and maintain accessibility under the “Leave no one behind” strategy. Highlights the importance of access to quality information, social inclusion, and financial literacy to empower informed customer decisions.
text:
Negative impacts  relate to practices that compromise fairness, inclusivity, and data security and can harm 
customer wellbeing, damage our reputation, and expose us to financial and regulatory risks. The negative 
impacts are not widespread or systemic, but based on individual incidents and link to the following topics:
•Access to quality information : There are potential negative impacts related to ‘Unfair Customer 
Treatment’, due to mis-selling, as well as ING (deliberately) misrepresenting a financial product or 
providing an unclear or unfair presentation of the financial product. These practices might lead to 
customers making uninformed decisions, potentially leading to financial distress. 
•Social inclusion: There are potential negative impacts on our customers due to non-discrimination 
violations and ING’s failure to provide access to products and services. This may result in the exclusion of 
customers due to accessibility barriers or regional restrictions, unequal treatment among customers, and 
the mis-selling of products through misleading marketing•Privacy: There are potential negative impacts related to data privacy in accordance with existing data 
protection legislation (e.g.  GDPR ). Failure to protect our clients’ data can negatively impact our customers 
and may result in identity theft, financial loss due to fraudulent activities, loss of privacy, and emotional 
distress.Risks  arise from the materialisation of the identified negative impacts and are associated with failing to 
uphold fairness, inclusivity, and data security.  
Assessment of current financial effects are based on the engagement with our customers, mainly through 
our complaints channels and our legal claims processes. We rely on the existing approach based on the 
recognition and measurement criteria of provisions in the Financial Statements, for more information see 
Note 15 'Provisions' and Note 41 'Legal proceedings' . For 2024, there are no significant current financial 
effects.

title: Processes for engaging with customers
heading: 5.2.2 Processes for engaging with customers
start_phrase: At ING, we regularly engage with our customers in order to understand any concerns they may have and to improve our services and activities.
summary:
- Scope and focus: Addresses consumers and end-users of ING’s services, centering on private individual customers in Retail Banking per a double materiality assessment. Commits to fair access, transparent communication, and respect for customer rights.
- Vulnerable customers: Recognizes customers who may be at heightened risk (e.g., elderly; those with temporary or permanent sensory, physical, cognitive, neurodiverse disabilities; chronic illness; reading difficulties) and the need for heightened care.
- Identified negative impacts:
  - Access to quality information: Risk of unfair treatment through mis-selling, misrepresentation, or unclear product information leading to uninformed decisions and potential financial distress.
  - Social inclusion: Risks from discrimination, accessibility barriers, regional restrictions, unequal treatment, and misleading marketing that can exclude customers.
  - Privacy: Data protection failures (e.g., GDPR breaches) could cause identity theft, financial loss, loss of privacy, and emotional distress.
- Risks and financial effects: Risks arise from failures in fairness, inclusivity, and data security. Financial effects are assessed via customer engagement, complaints, and legal claims; provisions follow Financial Statements Notes 15 and 41. No significant current financial effects reported for 2024.
- Customer engagement and oversight: Ongoing engagement led by the head of Retail; annual Net Promoter Score tracking; complaints channels inform impact and remediation. The Global Centre of Expertise (CoE) Accessibility supports inclusive, accessible product and service development.
- External accessibility initiatives: Active participation in global accessibility forums (Zero Project Annual Conference, European Platform for Rehabilitation, Social Services Europe). Insights guide adjustments across ING. Efforts include the EAA Compliance Program and a January 2024 joint report with Sia-Partners on the European Accessibility Act’s impact on banking services.
- Customer strategy (Superior customer value): Aims to make banking easy, instant, personal, and relevant; ensure clear pricing, plain language, and continuous accessibility. The “Leave no one behind” strategy promotes inclusion for customers with and without disabilities. Emphasizes financial literacy to support informed decisions and financial health.
text:
Processes for engaging with customers
At ING, we regularly engage with our customers in order to understand any concerns they may have and to 
improve our services and activities. This engagement is the responsibility of our head of Retail. One of the 
ways we engage with our customers is through the measurement of our yearly net promoter score (NPS). 
For more information on our NPS, see the ‘ Superior customer value ’ section. Furthermore, we continue to 
encourage inclusive and accessible product and service development throughout ING, with the support of 
ING’s Global Centre of Ex pertise (CoE) Accessibility. In addition to our general engagement activities, we use 
our complaints channels to gain a clearer picture of the impacts we have on our customers. See our 
complaints and remediation process  in this section for more information.
Global CoE Accessibility is an active member of the global accessibility community, by, for example, sending 
speakers to events attended by experts in the field and representatives of disability interest groups/
organisations. The conferences where ING participated in 2024 were the Zero Project Annual Conference in 
Vienna, the European Platform for Rehabilitation Annual Conference and the Social Services Europe Annual 
Conference. These conferences offer insights into new innovations and how these are received by users. 
There’s also the opportunity to learn about the challenges people with all kinds of disabilities encounter, and 
the new developments that might cause concern. With the information acquired, ING can adjust its actions 
and influence ING entities to do the same. The efforts of our strategic vision and the EAA Compliance 
Program resulted in, among other things, the publication of our joint report with consultancy firm Sia-
Partners in January 2024, on the impact of the EAA on banking services.

title: Customer strategy - Superior customer value
heading: 5.2.3 Customer strategy - Superior customer value
start_phrase: We strive to make banking easy, instant, personal and relevant so customers can stay up to date with all that ING offers.
summary:
- Scope and focus: Addresses consumers and end-users of ING’s services, prioritizing private individuals in Retail Banking per double materiality. Emphasis on fair access, transparent communication, and respect for customer rights.
- Vulnerable customers: Defines vulnerability (e.g., elderly; temporary/permanent sensory, physical, cognitive, neurodiverse disabilities; chronic disease; reading difficulties) and tailors care to prevent harm or exclusion.
- Key impacts and risks:
  - Access to quality information: Risks of unfair customer treatment and mis-selling leading to uninformed decisions and possible financial distress.
  - Social inclusion: Potential discrimination, accessibility barriers, regional restrictions, unequal treatment, and misleading marketing.
  - Privacy: Data protection risks under laws like GDPR, with potential identity theft, fraud, loss of privacy, and emotional distress.
  - Financial effects: Monitored via complaints and legal processes; no significant current financial effects reported for 2024.
- Customer engagement and accessibility:
  - Ongoing engagement led by the head of Retail; uses NPS and complaints to identify issues and improve services.
  - Global Centre of Expertise Accessibility participates in international forums, informs actions, supports EAA compliance, and co-published a 2024 report on EAA impacts (with Sia-Partners).
- Customer strategy – Superior customer value: Aims to make banking easy, instant, personal, and relevant; clear pricing and accessible communication; “Leave no one behind” accessibility strategy; promotes financial literacy; integrates privacy/data security and regulatory updates into risk and compliance frameworks.
- Governance and policy framework:
  - Customer Centricity Policy (CCP) rolled out globally in 2024 to prevent mis-selling/unfair treatment and ensure equitable access, including for persons with disabilities.
  - Integrates new regulations (e.g., European Accessibility Act, Consumer Credit Directive, Retail Investor Strategy) via governance measures, policy reviews, risk assessments, and control processes like the Product Approval and Review Process (PARP).
  - Sets minimum standards: act in customers’ and society’s interests; aligned complaint processes; clear, accessible, non-misleading information; suitability and needs assessment across the product lifecycle; consideration of ESG risks and customer impacts.
  - While no standalone customer human rights policy, seeks alignment through EU financial directives (e.g., IDD, MiFID). CCP to be enhanced in 2025 with minimum standards on non-discrimination and access to basic banking.
- Complaints and remediation:
  - CCP mandates transparent, accessible complaints processes across channels (assisted and self-service), regular assessment, and root-cause analysis.
  - Complaints can be filed via ING or third parties; anti-retaliation upheld via Whistleblower policy.
  - Resolution aims at first contact; escalations handled by specialized teams; outcomes can include product/process changes, compensation, and apologies; performance tracked via resolution timeliness and frequency to drive structural improvements.

title: Customer Centricity Policy
heading: 5.2.4.1 Customer Centricity Policy
start_phrase: ING offers a large variety of financial products and services to customers, and so we face different risks and are subject to a multitude of regulations.
summary:
- Focus on customer-centric compliance covering non-discrimination, equitable access to products and services, responsible marketing, and strong privacy/data security, managed through ongoing regulatory monitoring and integrated risk/compliance processes.
- Human rights considerations inform strategy and business model; governance roles and responsibilities referenced in sustainability governance.
- Customer Centricity Policy (CCP) rolled out globally in 2024 to prevent mis-selling and unfair treatment and ensure accessible, suitable, and fairly priced products throughout the customer lifecycle.
- CCP embeds governance to implement evolving regulations (e.g., European Accessibility Act, Consumer Credit Directive, Retail Investor Strategy), with continuous policy reviews, risk assessments, and regulatory change management.
- Requirements include: clear, non-misleading product information; PARP oversight; trained professionals; consideration of ESG risks and impacts; global minimum standards on product suitability, standardized complaints handling, accessible information, and assessment of individual customer needs to reduce financial distress.
- Alignment with human rights through EU financial market directives (IDD, MiFID), with planned 2025 CCP enhancements to set minimum standards on accessibility, non-discrimination, and access to basic banking across all countries.
- Complaints and remediation framework: transparent, multi-channel access (assisted and self-service), progress updates, regular assessments and root-cause analyses, ability to complain via third parties, and no-retaliation protections via the whistleblower policy.
- Operational handling aims for first-contact resolution with escalation to specialized teams, monitoring of resolution times and rates, and remedies including product/process changes, financial compensation, and apologies, using complaint insights to drive structural improvements.
text:
Customer Centricity Policy
ING offers a large variety of financial products and services to customers, and so we face different risks and 
are subject to a multitude of regulations. Our Customer Centricity Policy (CCP) helps in preventing and 
mitigating impacts and risks regarding the topics of social inclusion and access to quality information, 
including mis-selling and unfair customer treatment. For instance, we want all our customers to have 
equitable access to our products and services, including persons with disabilities, which is why we strive to 
comply with the procedures of our policies and apply controls. 
We rolled out the CCP to all countries in 2024. In alignment with the CCP, we have governance measures in 
place to integrate new rules and regulations, such as the European Accessibility Act, the Consumer Credit 
Directive, and the Retail Investor Strategy, into our business processes and control environment. Our 
governance framework, supported by continuous policy reviews, risk assessments, and regulatory change 
implementation, enables us to address material risks related to discrimination, inclusivity, and access to 
information in a timely and effective manner. 
The CCP defines high-level obligations aiming to ensure ING handles risks in line with regulations 
appropriately. We want to offer products and services suitable for our customers throughout the whole 
relationship lifecycle at a fair price considering the market, costs and risks. We monitor internal controls and 
processes, such as our Product Review and Approval Process (PARP), in which all elements of customer 
centricity are considered and challenged. The CCP requires us to communicate information on products and 
services in a clear and non-misleading manner, and provide services and trusted advice through 
professionals with the necessary knowledge and expertise. In doing so, we also consider the ESG risks and 
impact of our products and services on customers.Having a global CCP enables us to align and assess whether customer centricity is applied to all products and 
customers across the globe. Norms that we have formalised into minimum standards include the need to 
only create and sell products that are in the interests of customers and society, to have an aligned standard 
on complaint s processes, to provide clear and accessible information that is at all times fair and not 
misleading, and to assess the needs of individual customers both when we sell a product and when the 
customer uses a product. With this, we aim to mitigate potential and actual financial distress for individual 
customers, resulting from not having access to products, services and/or quality information.  
While we do not have a human rights policy commitment in relation to our customers, ING seeks alignment 
with fundamental rights through the implementation  of relevant financial markets EU directives such as IDD 
and MiFID , which reference human rights in the preamble. In 2025, our CCP will be enhanced further and 
updated on the accessibility of our products and services, to establish minimum compliance standards on 
non-discriminatio n and access to banking (basic needs) across all countries.

title: Complaints and remediation process
heading: 5.2.4.2 Complaints and remediation process
start_phrase: In addition to our general engagement activities, we use our complaints channels to gain a clearer picture of the impacts we have on our customers.
summary:
- Emphasis on customer-centric compliance and risk management integrated into existing frameworks, prioritizing non-discrimination, access to products and information, responsible marketing, and robust privacy/data security, with continuous regulatory monitoring.
- Governance context: human rights inform strategy and business model; oversight and roles addressed in sustainability governance.
- Customer Centricity Policy (CCP): rolled out globally in 2024; sets minimum standards for fair treatment, suitability, fair pricing, clear/non-misleading information, and aligned complaints processes; embeds ESG considerations and uses Product Approval and Review Process (PARP); governance to implement EU rules (European Accessibility Act, Consumer Credit Directive, Retail Investor Strategy); alignment with IDD/MiFID preambles in lieu of a dedicated customer human rights policy; planned 2025 enhancement to set minimum standards on accessibility, non-discrimination, and basic access to banking.
- Complaints and remediation: multi-channel access (assisted and self-service), transparency and status updates, regular assessments with root cause analysis, escalation to specialized teams, remedies (product changes, compensation, apologies), and structural improvements; anti-retaliation covered under Whistleblower policy; standardized complaint labels (human rights, accessibility, privacy, ESG, customer centricity) to go live in 2025 to improve root cause analysis and identify severe human rights incidents.
- Social inclusion and access to quality information: accessibility measures (voice-activated ATMs, notched cards, relay/sign-language services, accessible websites and apps with screen readers); EU-wide EAA compliance program targeted for completion in 2025; initiatives under UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking and the Commitment to Financial Health and Inclusion, including tools to build savings and manage expenses; monitoring of channel availability and service uptime; ongoing compliance monitoring, issue management, and periodic product reviews via PARP that may lead to remediation.
- Global Personal Data Protection Internal Policy (GPDP): GDPR-aligned policy governing lawful, purpose-limited, necessary, and accurate personal data processing; operational flows to fulfill data subject rights (access, erasure, objection, correction) timely; transparency on data use and sharing; ensuring equivalent protections with third parties and for cross-border transfers outside the EEA.
text:
Complaints and remediation process
In addition to our general engagement activities, we use our complaints channels to gain a clearer picture of 
the impacts we have on our customers. The insights we obtain into complaints can help us to implement 
structural changes in our products and processes. The CCP sets out the minimum requirements for 
complaints procedures in all ING entities, including the need to be transparent about the complaints process 
and to keep customers informed of the progress in ING’s handling of a complaint. All complaints must be 
assessed regularly, and root cause analyses must be carried out to mitigate the risks of customer harm. The 
CCP also ensures that customers can raise complaints about ING’s financial products through third parties, 
including distributors, brokers and manufacturers. There are several ways our customers can file a 
complaint. Within nearly all our Retail markets there is at least one assisted channel available (e.g. call 
centre, branch, human chat, social media), and at least one self-service channel (e.g. mail, e-mail, online 
channels app and web) where customers can file a complaint which will then be handled by a human agent.
Customers are made aware of these channels  via publicly available information e.g. websites of ING (FAQs 
and search engine) and via the Terms & Conditions provided to customers during onboarding. Furthermore, 
a call centre, branch and/or a chat agent can provide further information regarding the complaints 
processes when a customer contacts ING. We value our customers and evaluate their concerns seriously 
and, while not embedded in our customer -focused  policies, we do not tolerate retaliation by any employee . 
For our anti-retaliation measures included in our Whistleblower policy, see the ‘ Business conduct ’ chapter. 
We manage complaints primarily through contact centres and when possible complaints are solved upon 
initial contact. If unresolved, they escalate to specialised teams. We evaluate the complaints handling 
process, for instance, through an assessment of the time it takes to resolve complaints and how frequently 
we do so. A change in products, financial compensation and/or apologies can help to address any negative 
impacts on customers. We analyse complaints to implement structural changes in products, processes, Contents ING at a glance Strategy, business model 
and value creationOur financial performance Our leadership and
